meta.title: Bank & NBFC Audit Casebook
meta.huntQuestion: Which rule or requirement decides this?
meta.tagline: Spot the requirement. *Then* write the answer.
meta.intro: {cases} cases on bank and NBFC audit from the study material, RTPs and past papers. Name the rule, then check ICAI's answer.

P.label: Special audit factors
P.title: Why banks need special audit consideration
P.short: Characteristics that drive bank audit risk
P.law: Banks differ from other commercial enterprises: custody of large volumes of cash and negotiable instruments; a huge volume and variety of transactions needing complex IT-heavy accounting and controls; a wide network of geographically dispersed branches with decentralised authority; off-balance-sheet commitments that may involve no accounting entry; transactions initiated at one location, recorded at another and managed at a third; and transactions initiated and completed by the customer alone (ATM/net/mobile banking) without any bank employee's intervention.
notes: Special audit considerations arise from: the particular nature of risks in banking transactions; the scale of operations and resultant large exposures that can build up fast; extensive dependence on IT; the effect of statutory/regulatory requirements; and continuing new products outpacing accounting/auditing practice.

The auditor must have detailed knowledge of the products a bank offers and the risks they carry, and understand interface controls between the bank's different applications (data flows from one system to another).

Cue for the examiner: a vignette describing deposits/treasury/credit recovery/internal accounts almost always signals this provision's framing paragraph, not a standalone test — read on for which specific area is actually being tested.

P.label: Legal framework
P.title: Statutes governing banks in India
P.short: BR Act, RBI Act and the other Acts
P.law: The principal enactments governing banks: the Banking Regulation Act, 1949; the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (gives RBI wide powers of direction over banks); the State Bank of India Act, 1955; the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970 and 1980; the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976; the Companies Act, 2013; the Information Technology Act, 2000; the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002; SARFAESI Act, 2002; the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005; the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007; and the Co-operative Societies Act, 1912 for co-operative banks.
notes: The BR Act, 1949 prescribes the Third Schedule formats (Form A balance sheet, Form B P&L) and s.30 audit requirement; the RBI Act, 1934 is the source of RBI's directions power over all banks, not only banking companies.
SARFAESI, 2002 and the PMLA, 2002 matter for NPA recovery/securitisation and KYC/AML respectively — see Beyond the SM: SARFAESI.
Co-operative banks additionally answer to the Co-operative Societies Act / State Co-operative Societies Acts — see Beyond the SM: co-operative bank audit.
P.mem: BR-RBI-SBI-BC(70/80)-RRB-Cos-IT-PMLA-SARFAESI-CIC-PSS-CoOp: the legal-framework diagram in the SM, in the order it is drawn.

P.label: Form & content of FS
P.title: Third Schedule format and standalone vs consolidated FS
P.short: Form A/B and branch consolidation
P.law: Every banking company must prepare a Balance Sheet and P&L in the forms of the Third Schedule to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (Form A: Balance Sheet; Form B: P&L), or as near thereto as circumstances admit, and must also comply with the Accounting Standards specified under s.133 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 7 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 (Ind AS implementation is deferred by RBI for scheduled commercial banks).
notes: Preparing a bank's balance sheet usually means preparing standalone financial statements (consolidating branch accounts and verticals/departments — procedures vary bank to bank) and, separately, consolidated financial statements.
Private banks centralise accounting — there is no mandatory branch audit concept for them under RBI guidelines, unlike public sector/nationalised banks.
Public sector and private banks listed on a recognised stock exchange must additionally comply with SEBI LODR.

P.label: Appointment of SCAs/SBAs
P.title: Appointing statutory central and branch auditors
P.short: Who appoints, what the letter contains
P.law: Section 30(1), Banking Regulation Act, 1949 requires the balance sheet and P&L of a banking company to be audited by a person qualified to audit companies. Most nationalised/public-sector banks appoint four or more firms jointly as Statutory Central Auditors (SCAs) (number depends on size/Board decision per RBI guidelines); statutory branch audit (SBA) is always carried out by a single firm.
notes: The appointment letter typically covers: period of appointment; particulars of other central auditors and of previous auditors; procedural requirements for accepting the assignment (letter of acceptance — disqualification averment, conduct of audit, confirmation of name/constitution/address, fidelity-and-secrecy declaration, restriction on accepting other assignments from the bank); division of work and reporting responsibilities among joint auditors (nationalised banks, usually fixed later); and scope including any special reports/certificates beyond the main report.
SBA letters are on similar lines but drop the "other central auditors"/"division of work" items (a branch has one auditor).

Authority appointing: a banking company's auditor is appointed at the shareholders' AGM; a nationalised bank's auditor is appointed by the Board. Either way, RBI approval is required before appointment.

Declaration of indebtedness: before appointing SCAs/SBAs, RBI requires a written confirmation that the auditor/firm/partners/family are not declared wilful defaulters by any bank/FI — in addition to the s.141 Companies Act, 2013 disqualification declaration.
Bar on internal assignments: a firm cannot take the statutory audit of a bank while associated with internal assignments in that bank during the same year.

Clause (8), Part I, First Schedule to the CA Act, 1949 — a CA in practice cannot accept the position of auditor previously held by another CA without first communicating with that auditor in writing (applies on taking over SCA/SBA appointment too).

P.label: Audit stages (5)
P.title: The five stages of a bank audit
P.short: Initial → Understanding → Risk → Execution → Reporting
P.law: A bank audit proceeds through Stage I Initial considerations, Stage II Understanding, Stage III Risk assessment, Stage IV Execution, Stage V Reporting.
notes: Stage I: acceptance & continuance, declaration of indebtedness, bar on internal assignments, SA 210 terms of engagement, communication with previous auditor, planning, establishing the engagement team.

Stage II: understanding the bank and its environment including internal control; understanding the accounting process; understanding the risk management process (oversight by TCWG, identification/measurement/monitoring of risk, control activities, monitoring activities, reliable information systems).

Stage III: identifying and assessing risks of material misstatement (SA 315); assessing fraud risk including money laundering (SA 240, RBI KYC/AML guidelines); assessing specific industry/IT risks; risk from outsourcing of activities.

Stage IV: engagement team discussions; designing responses to assessed risk (SA 330); establishing the overall audit strategy (SA 300); the Audit Planning Memorandum; determining audit materiality; considering going concern.
Stage V: reporting — see Auditor's report and LFAR.

P.label: Initial considerations
P.title: Declaration of indebtedness & the internal-assignments bar
P.short: Before you even accept the bank audit
P.law: RBI requires every statutory central/branch auditor to give a written declaration of indebtedness (not a wilful defaulter of any bank/FI) before appointment, in addition to the s.141 Companies Act disqualification declaration. RBI has also decided that audit firms must not hold the statutory audit while associated with internal assignments in the same bank in the same year.
notes: SA 210 requires agreeing the terms of engagement before significant fieldwork begins — usually an engagement letter, written by the auditor, acknowledged by the bank.
Clause (8), Part I, First Schedule, CA Act, 1949: must communicate in writing with the previous auditor before accepting the position.

P.label: Bank risk assessment
P.title: SA 315, SA 240 and outsourcing risk
P.short: Risk of material misstatement, fraud & outsourcing
P.law: SA 315 requires identifying and assessing risks of material misstatement at the financial-statement and assertion levels. SA 240 requires the auditor to identify and assess the risk of fraud, including money laundering, maintaining professional scepticism throughout. RBI's KYC/AML guidelines ("Know Your Customer – Anti-Money Laundering Standards") require banks to have policies, procedures and controls to deter, recognise and report money-laundering activity.
notes: Outsourcing risk: banks increasingly outsource for cost/expertise, but this creates risk the auditor must specifically evaluate — the bank must still effectively manage the risk even though the activity itself is delegated.
SA 330 then requires designing and performing audit procedures responsive to the assessed risks.

P.label: IT environment
P.title: Key security controls the auditor should check
P.short: CBS-era controls checklist
P.law: Because audit must be conducted through the bank's systems, the auditor needs the bank's overall IT policy/structure, data-processing and interface controls, data integrity/security, BCP/DR plans, the accounting manual, controls over key account-head usage and expense booking, controls on e-banking/internet channels, MIS reports and major exception reports.
notes: Key security controls to verify: authorised/accurate/complete data for processing; system restarts without distortion after failure; no unauthorised program amendments; access controls match job responsibilities and are segregated (front/back office); authenticated parameter/user-level changes; manually calculated charges are accounted and authorised; exceptional transaction reports authorised/verified daily; account master/balance changes restricted to authorised personnel; HO-authorised GL codes exist in the system; GL reconciles with subsidiary books.

Overall IT review is a head-office-level responsibility (SCA); branch auditors generally lack access to bank-wide IT policy and instead carry out data review/testing at branch level using SCA guidance, sharing results upward.

P.label: Internal audit/RBIA
P.title: Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA)
P.short: Centralised inspection, concurrent-auditor oversight
P.law: A bank's central audit/inspection department (headed by a Chief Audit Executive) is a part-centralised, part-decentralised function responsible for Risk-Based Internal Audit as per the RBI framework, plus identifying branches for revenue audit, appointing concurrent auditors, setting their scope and reviewing their work.
notes: RBIA's risk assessment: identify inherent business risk by branch activity; assess effectiveness of controls over those risks (control risk); assess overall level/direction of business and control risk; draw up a risk matrix by branch.

P.label: CRR & SLR requirements
P.title: Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio
P.short: Why banks hold CRR/SLR and how auditors verify it
P.law: CRR: a specified minimum fraction of total customer deposits banks must hold as reserves (cash, or deposit with RBI) — requirement in the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (banking companies) / RBI Act, 1934 (scheduled banks generally). SLR: every scheduled commercial bank must hold a prescribed share of liquid assets (gold, cash, approved government securities) before extending credit, so it can meet a sudden surge in depositor demand.
notes: RBI requires SCAs to verify SLR compliance on 12 odd dates in different months of the fiscal year, none of them a Friday; the report goes to top management and to RBI.

Audit procedure: obtain the relevant RBI circulars (esp. the DTL composition rules); request branch auditors to send weekly Friday trial balances (consolidated at HO to fix the DTL position each reporting Friday) and verify branch cash balances on selected dates; test-check the HO's DTL consolidation against branch returns; check securities valuation against RBI guidelines; verify Form A (CRR) and Form VIII (SLR) return correctness on a sample basis.
Automated Data Flow (ADF) is now used for CRR/SLR reporting — auditors must design procedures around it.
See DTL computation for the exclusions/inclusions that drive the CRR/SLR denominator.

P.label: DTL computation
P.title: What's excluded from, and included in, Demand & Time Liabilities
P.short: The DTL adjustment list examiners love
P.law: DTL (Demand and Time Liabilities) is the base on which CRR/SLR are computed. Starting from the bank's reported liability figure, specific items must be excluded and specific items must be included as per RBI guidelines, regardless of how the bank's own books show them.
notes: Excluded from DTL: paid-up capital, reserves, any credit balance in the P&L account; loans taken from RBI, and refinance from EXIM Bank/NHB/NABARD/SIDBI; bills discounted by the bank with eligible FIs approved by RBI; net income-tax provision; amounts received from DICGC/ECGC pending claim adjustment; amounts received from court receivers; net unrealised gain/loss on trading-portfolio derivatives; income received in advance (non-refundable fees/charges); liabilities from utilising the Bankers' Acceptance Facility (BAF); part-recoveries from borrowers on debts considered bad/doubtful; amounts in Indian currency against import bills held pending final rates; unadjusted link-branch balances for agency business; margins held in sundry deposits for funded facilities.

Included in DTL even if not yet booked: the net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts (credit entries outstanding >5 years are taken at gross); interest accrued on deposits, calculated each reporting fortnight per the applicable method whether or not yet accounted for in the books — so the bank's true liability is fairly reflected; cash collaterals received under collateralised derivative transactions (an 'outside liability'); borrowings from abroad, taken at gross as 'liabilities to other' (unlike liabilities to the banking system in India, which may be netted against banking-system assets in India) — so an adverse Nostro Mirror Account balance is a 'liability to other'.
Foreign-currency items are converted using the RBI/FBIL reference rate (New York closing rate as fallback).
P.mem: Exclude: capital, reserves, P&L credit, RBI loan, EXIM/NHB/NABARD/SIDBI refinance, bad-debt recoveries, sundry-deposit margins. Include: branch-adjustment credit balance, interest accrued (even if unbooked).

P.label: General IC
P.title: General-purpose internal controls in a bank
P.short: Rotation, dual checking, stationery custody
P.law: Banks must implement and maintain a system of internal controls for risk mitigation, good governance and regulatory compliance.
notes: Staff/officers rotated between positions frequently and without prior notice; one person's work always checked by another (usually an officer); daily independent arithmetical checks; bank forms (cheque books, DD/pay-order books, traveller's cheques, forex cards) kept with one officer, issuance/stock verified by another; mail opened by a responsible officer, signatures checked against the signature book; signature/telegraphic code books kept by responsible officers with restricted access; insurance against fire/calamity/theft/employee infidelity; financial powers of officers clearly defined by grade; periodic surprise inspection of HO/branches with prompt rectification of flagged irregularities.
Trap: a lapse here (e.g. same official opening mail and lacking a signature book) is an internal-control deficiency to flag in the LFAR, even if no loss has yet occurred.

P.label: Internal control — cash
P.title: Joint custody and daily checking of cash
P.short: Cash custody controls
P.law: Cash is kept in the joint custody of two responsible officers; cash is test-checked daily and counted in full occasionally by an officer other than the handler; actual cash agrees with the day book daily.
notes: The cashier must have no access to the customer ledger or day book — a safeguard against losses, since banks are sometimes tempted to use cashiers as ledger clerks when short-staffed.

Cash-receipt-voucher counterfoils countersigned by a Cash Department officer in addition to the receiving cashier; payments only after vouchers are passed by an authorised officer and entered in the customer's account; receipt/payment scroll totals compared to the day book's cash column by an independent person; high-value cash receipts/payments verified by a senior officer/branch manager, excess cash remitted to the currency chest per the branch's retention limit daily.

P.label: IC — clearing/bills
P.title: CTS clearing, bills for collection and bills purchased
P.short: Cheque Truncation System and bill custody
P.law: Under the Cheque Truncation System (CTS), an electronic image of the cheque (with MICR data, presentation date, presenting bank) is sent to the paying branch via the clearing house, eliminating physical movement.
notes: Inward clearing of ₹5 lakh and above: RBI requires the branch to call/email the customer; auditor test-checks compliance. Signatures must be verified on every cheque; unpaid outward-clearing cheques are sent to the customer or they are told to collect.

Bills for collection: documents received/entered by a responsible officer and dispatched complete; customer/principal credited only after collection or an advice of collection; a bill sent by one branch to another for collection must not be double-counted in the amalgamated balance sheet — the receiving branch reverses such entries at year end.

Bills purchased: officer verifies title documents are properly assigned; sufficient margin kept to cover value decline; if the bank can't collect on due date, immediate recovery steps from the drawer against security; irregular outstandings reported to HO; discount on bills outstanding at year end is apportioned between the two years.

P.label: IC — advances
P.title: Documentation, margins, drawing power and limits
P.short: Advances internal-control checklist
P.law: Advances only after the bank satisfies itself of borrower creditworthiness and obtains proper sanction; documents (agreements, DPNs, hypothecation letters) executed before disbursal; sufficient margin kept against security to cover decline in value and meet RBI directives (margin set by proper authority, generally or per-account); securities received/returned by a responsible officer and kept in joint custody of two officers; registrable securities registered in the bank's name (or accompanied by sufficient title documents).
notes: Accounts must stay within both the drawing power and the sanctioned limit; an additional temporary limit may be sanctioned for a maximum of 20% of the existing limit and 90 days' tenure; excesses are reported to Management/HO regularly; each advance account's operation is reviewed at least once a year.

This is the provision an RTP/PYQ internal-control case usually tests via a fact pattern listing 3–5 lapses (credit appraisal, documentation, joint custody, drawing-power breach not reported) — see RTP Sep 2025 Q16.
P.mem: 20% / 90 days: the temporary-limit numbers examiners love to test.

P.label: IC — credit cards
P.title: Credit card operations internal control
P.short: Issue, settlement and recovery controls
P.law: Effective screening of applications with sound credit assessment; strict control over card storage/issue; a system for merchants to confirm unutilised limit before accepting a settlement above a specified % of the cardholder's total limit; prompt merchant reporting of accepted settlements; reimbursement only after verifying validity of the merchant's acceptance, and charged (gross of commission) immediately to the customer's account; statements sent regularly/promptly; monitoring/follow-up of payments; overdue payments beyond a reasonable period identified and acted on, with credit stopped via merchant bulletins for defaulters; periodic review of cardholder accounts (limit revision, doubtful-amount determination and provisioning).
notes: A recurring exam fact pattern: "evaluate the internal control system for credit card operations" — answer by walking through this full list, not just the storage point.

P.label: Verify — cash
P.title: Cash, RBI balance, other banks, money at call
P.short: Existence & completeness objective
P.law: The Third Schedule requires disclosure of cash, balances with RBI, balances with other banks and money at call & short notice. The auditor's basic objective is existence and completeness at balance sheet date.
notes: Physically verify cash (incl. foreign currency, ATM/CDM cash) as close to balance-sheet date as possible; agree to the cash register/CBS balance.

RBI balance: verify against bank confirmation certificates and reconciliation statements; review reconciling items — unresponded cash transactions, items needing write-off, and other entries unresponded for more than 15 days.

Other-bank balances: additionally check no outstanding debit/credit for charges or interest; no outstanding clearing cheques; outstation cheques sent for collection credited subsequently; examine large inter-bank transactions for year-end window dressing. Convert foreign balances at the balance-sheet-date rate.

Money at call/short notice: check authorisation and compliance with HO limits (incl. inter-bank call-money limits); verify against borrower certificates/call-loan receipts; agree register totals to the general ledger control account; call loans cannot be netted against call loans received; verify year-end interest accrual.

P.label: Verify — invest
P.title: Classification, valuation and physical verification of investments
P.short: HTM/HFT/AFS, NPI, PMS certificates
P.law: The auditor's primary objective: existence, ownership and valuation, plus compliance with RBI's investment-policy master circular (statutory/regulatory non-compliance can directly and materially misstate the financial statements).
notes: Review the investment policy for conformity with RBI guidelines; check segregation of front/middle/back office functions; examine reconciliation of the investment account, physical verification of scrips, BR/SGL confirmations.

Classification: the entire portfolio must sit in one of three categories — HTM (Held to Maturity), HFT (Held for Trading), AFS (Available for Sale) — fixed at acquisition by Board/ALCO/Investment Committee decision; shifting AFS→HTM needs Board approval.
NPI (Non-Performing Investment): interest/principal in arrears, unpaid for more than 90 days — income is not recognised and depreciation provision is required.

Physical verification of scrips at year-end close of business, or via PDO/custodian/depository statements; for BRs (Bank Receipts) held at year end, obtain counterparty confirmation and investigate long-outstanding BRs; BRs cannot be issued for government-securities transactions where SGL facility is available.

Half-yearly reviews (30 Sept and 31 March) of the investment portfolio are mandatory, covering operational aspects and policy-adherence certification; internal auditors separately conduct concurrent audit of treasury transactions, reported to the CMD monthly.
PMS/other-constituent investments need separate accounts, and PMS investments require a separate external audit.

P.label: Verify — advances
P.title: What the auditor of advances is really checking
P.short: Existence, validity, valuation, classification, provisioning
P.law: The auditor seeks evidence that: amounts shown are outstanding at balance-sheet date; advances represent amounts due to the bank, supported by loan documents; there are no unrecorded advances; the valuation basis is appropriate (recoverability reflected); disclosure/classification follows accounting policy and regulatory requirements; and provisions are made per RBI norms/ASs/GAAP.
notes: Evaluation of internal control: credit appraisal followed; sanction within delegated authority; documents executed before disbursal; sanction terms/end-use complied with (esp. term loans); security existence/enforceability/valuation (incl. registration); validity of recorded amounts; unauthorised overdrawings flagged on review; review/renewal system followed; drawing power recalculated per stock/book-debt statements per sanction letter; compliance with Loan Policy and RBI prudential norms.

Substantive procedures: verify CBS master-data correctness (instalments/EMI/rate/tenure); single customer ID across all facilities; examine all large advances, sample the rest; examine SMA-1/SMA-2 accounts not yet NPA; examine accounts adversely flagged by concurrent/internal/RBI inspection; check restructured-account compliance and additional provisioning; examine quick/early-mortality accounts (NPA within 12 months of sanction); verify interest completeness/accuracy; analytical procedures.
Recoverability: review periodic borrower compliance statements, latest financials, security-inspection reports, and auditor's reports of borrowers with credit facilities beyond a board-fixed cut-off.

P.label: Drawing power
P.title: How drawing power (DP) is computed
P.short: Stock/debtors, less margin, less creditors for stock
P.law: Drawing power is calculated per the extant Credit Policy/sanction letter, agreed with the auditor. Declared stock must not include the amount of any sundry creditors for goods (or goods covered by LCs/guarantees) already availed — i.e. net stock value for DP = stock paid for, net of such creditors. Where security is book debts, net eligible debtors (per sanction terms, less bills discounted with banks) is used. DP is calculated net of the stipulated margin.
notes: Stock statements relied on for DP must be no older than 3 months; outstanding based on an older statement is irregular.
Consortium accounts: the lead bank's DP calculation/allocation is binding on member banks.
Working-capital advances to construction businesses: value WIP consistently, and reduce DP for any mobilisation advance received.
Stock audit (incl. book debts) is mandatory above a stipulated funded-exposure limit; the auditor reviews the stock auditor's valuation/DP comments.

Worked example (PYQ May 2025 Q10–11, Indore Main branch, Kiran Ltd): Stock ₹900L (incl. ₹60L damaged), Receivables ₹800L (₹100L >90 days overdue), Creditors for stock ₹140L, margin 25% on stock / 40% on receivables, CC limit ₹1,000L. DP = [(900 − 60 damaged − 140 creditors) × 75%] + [(800 − 100 overdue) × 60%] = 525 + 420 = ₹945 lakh (capped by the ₹1,000L limit, so unaffected here).
P.mem: Net stock (paid-for, less creditors) × (1 − margin) + eligible debtors × (1 − margin).

P.label: Verify — fixed assets
P.title: Premises and other fixed assets
P.short: Section 9 holding-period bar, revaluation
P.law: The Third Schedule requires fixed assets classified as Premises and Other Fixed Assets; leased assets/intangibles are shown separately. Section 9, BR Act, 1949 bars a banking company from holding immovable property for more than 7 years from acquisition, except for its own use.
notes: Verify opening balance to the register/ledger; new premises against authorisation/title deeds/payment record; self-constructed assets against contractor bills/work orders; leasehold premium capitalisation/amortisation and improvements amortised over remaining useful life.
If title deeds are held at HO/elsewhere, obtain written branch management representation and mention in the main report and the LFAR.
Premises under construction shown separately; revaluation surplus/deficit and impairment tested against the applicable AS.

P.label: Verify — other assets
P.title: Inter-office adjustments, TDS, stationery, NBA, suspense
P.short: The residual 'other assets' head
P.law: Includes inter-office adjustments (debit balance), interest accrued, tax paid in advance/TDS, stationery & stamps, non-banking assets (NBA) acquired in satisfaction of claims, and a residual "Others" (unreceived claims, prepaid expenses, accrued non-interest income, etc.).
notes: Inter-office adjustments: report the year-end reconciliation status and ageing of outstanding debit/credit entries.
NBA: recorded at the lower of net book value of the advance or net realisable value of the asset acquired; ownership must be legally vested in the bank; Section 9 holding-period rule applies.
Suspense accounts: a classic fraud vector (unauthorised account opening/operation to disguise NPAs) — the auditor examines old outstandings and whether provision/write-off was made.

P.label: Asset classification
P.title: Standard, sub-standard, doubtful and loss assets
P.short: The four buckets and the NPA trigger
P.law: RBI's prudential norms classify advances into Standard, Sub-standard, Doubtful and Loss assets, based on the degree of credit weakness and dependence on collateral. An account is an NPA once income ceases to be generated for the bank per RBI's overdue/past-due norms. Asset classification is borrower-wise, not facility-wise: if one facility goes bad, all facilities to that borrower are treated as NPA.
notes: Accounts regularised near balance-sheet date: not automatically NPA if genuinely regularised, but the auditor assesses whether repayment was from genuine sources (not fresh bank funding) and whether inherent weakness persists.

Accounts with temporary deficiencies (DP based on a stock statement that's gone stale, balance temporarily over the limit, non-renewal on the due date) are not NPA merely for that reason — provided the stock statement relied on is <3 months old and the account hasn't been out of order for >90 days.
Limits not reviewed within 180 days of the due date/ad hoc sanction date → NPA (watch for repetitive ad hoc/short reviews used to dodge this).

Government-guaranteed advances: for income recognition, interest isn't taken to income unless realised, guarantee or no. For asset classification, a Central-Government-guaranteed advance is NPA only once the guarantee is invoked and repudiated; this carve-out does not apply to State-Government guarantees, which follow the ordinary >90-day rule.

Restructured advances: can be restructured from Standard, Sub-standard or Doubtful (never with retrospective effect); a restructured Standard account is downgraded to Sub-standard; an NPA that's restructured stays in its existing NPA category.

Upgradation: examine every NPA→Standard upgrade for strict RBI-guideline compliance — watch for partial recoveries dressed up as full regularisation, or post-cut-off-date recoveries used to upgrade as at balance-sheet date.

P.label: NPA income
P.title: Realisation basis, not accrual
P.short: No income on an NPA until actually received
P.law: Once an account is NPA, interest/other income on it is recognised only on realisation, not accrual. Income on government/corporate-body securities can be accrued only where interest is serviced regularly (not in arrears); dividend income may be accrued once declared at the AGM, with the right to receive established.
notes: Trap: a bank that books dividend income on accrual before the AGM declaration is wrong, even if ultimately paid — see SM TYK Q1.

P.label: Sale/purchase of NPAs
P.title: Conditions for selling or buying an NPA
P.short: 2-year holding, cash-only, no reversal of excess provision
P.law: A bank may sell an NPA only if it: (a) has remained NPA in its books for at least 2 years; (b) is sold without recourse (entire credit risk transfers); (c) the bank assumes no residual legal/operational risk after sale; (d) is sold on a cash basis only, never at a contingent price, with the entire consideration received upfront; and (e) the bank hasn't bought back an NPA it originally sold.
notes: Sale below net book value (NBV): the shortfall is debited to that year's P&L.

Sale above NBV: the excess is not recognised as profit and the excess provision is not reversed — it is retained to meet shortfall/loss on sale of other NPAs (this exact point is the examiner's favourite trap, tested in RTP May 2025 Q16 and SM TYK Q10/14).

Purchase of an NPA: the purchasing bank applies its own classification-appropriate provisioning; recovery is first adjusted against acquisition cost, only the excess is profit; for capital adequacy, a 100% risk weight applies to NPAs purchased from other banks.
P.mem: Profit on sale → never booked, used to cushion other NPA losses. Loss on sale → booked immediately.

P.label: Std-asset provisioning
P.title: Standard-asset provisioning is still required
P.short: Variable rates by sector, as a matter of prudence
P.law: Even Standard assets require a prudential provision, at variable rates by sector for funded outstandings, per RBI norms.
notes: Bifurcation of standard advances into the correct sector/category must be checked and certified at branch level for the provision to be computed correctly.

P.label: Capital adequacy & CRAR
P.title: Basel III, Tier I/II capital and the CRAR formula
P.short: Minimum 9% CRAR, Tier I ≥ (per Basel norms)
P.law: CRAR (Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio) = Eligible Total Capital Funds ÷ (Risk-weighted assets + risk-adjusted off-balance-sheet items) × 100. RBI requires a minimum CRAR of 9% on an ongoing basis, computed per the Master Circular on Capital Adequacy / New Capital Adequacy Framework (NCAF), itself built on the Basel III accord.
notes: Tier I capital: mainly share capital and disclosed reserves — the highest-quality, fully loss-absorbing capital.
Tier II capital: certain reserves and subordinated debt — lower loss-absorption capacity than Tier I.
Basel III's three aims: improve the sector's shock-absorption capacity; improve risk management/governance; strengthen transparency/disclosure.

Risk weights turn a balance-sheet asset into its risk-weighted value for the CRAR denominator (e.g. a secured housing loan up to ₹75 lakh carries 50% risk weight, above ₹75 lakh 75%, commercial real estate 100% — so a ₹60 lakh housing loan contributes ₹30 lakh to risk-weighted assets).
Stress testing: all commercial banks (excluding RRBs/LABs) must run a Board-approved Stress Testing framework integrated into risk management.

P.label: Reserves & surplus
P.title: Statutory reserves, capital reserves, share premium
P.short: What the Reserves & Surplus head must disclose
P.law: Disclosed under 'Reserves and Surplus': Statutory Reserves, Capital Reserves, Share Premium, Revenue and Other Reserves (incl. Investment Fluctuation Reserve), and the P&L balance — with opening balance, additions and deductions shown separately for each.
notes: Verify opening balances against the prior audited balance sheet; additions/deductions against Board resolutions; statutory reserve/share-premium appropriations against the governing legislation (and any RBI exemption from transfer); overseas branches checked for compliance with foreign law too.

P.label: Deposits
P.title: CASA, term deposits and NRI accounts
P.short: Demand vs term, and the NRE/NRO/FCNR distinctions
P.law: Deposits are repayable on demand (current and savings accounts — CASA) or after a fixed term (term/fixed/recurring deposits). Foreign-currency deposits (FCNR) are opened by NRIs as fixed deposits only; NRE accounts (rupee-denominated) may be opened by NRIs/PIOs and are repatriable; NRO accounts may be opened by any non-resident and are not repatriable except current income, subject to conditions.
notes: Savings accounts are for individuals/HUF/approved institutions only — never for business/professional concerns, which use current accounts.
Inoperative/dormant: no transactions for over 2 years → treat as inoperative; revival needs proper authority, and a significant balance drop vs. last year warrants checking withdrawal authorisation.
Bulk deposits (₹2 crore and above, scheduled commercial banks): check the correct interest rate was offered; closure before maturity: check the foreclosure penalty was deducted.
FCNR interest is calculated on a 360-day year and converted to INR at the HO-notified rate, with gain/loss taken to P&L.

General: watch for deposits inflated near year-end via near-date overdrafts parked as deposits, reversed after year-close (window dressing — qualify the report if suspected); interest accrued-but-not-due on deposits goes under 'other liabilities', not clubbed with deposits.

P.label: Borrowings
P.title: RBI, other banks, other institutions, abroad
P.short: Disclosure split and the rediscount/refinance distinction
P.law: Disclosed as Borrowings in India (from RBI / other banks / other institutions & agencies) and Borrowings outside India, with secured borrowings separately noted. Inter-office transactions are not borrowings.
notes: A clear distinction must be drawn between 'rediscount' (does not figure under this head) and 'refinance' (does).
Call/short-notice borrowings checked for proper authorisation, rate and duration; external confirmations per SA 505 support significant-risk balances.

P.label: Other liabilities
P.title: Bills payable, inter-office adjustments, interest accrued
P.short: The 'other liabilities' residual head
P.law: Disclosed under 'Other Liabilities and Provisions': bills payable, inter-office adjustments (net, if credit), interest accrued, and others (including provisions).
notes: Bills payable controls: standard printed forms; unused forms held by a responsible officer; a reliable private code for telegrams known only to responsible officers; signatures on demand drafts checked against the specimen book; TTs/DDs immediately confirmed inter-branch, with a debit advice on payment.
The advances and investments figures on the balance sheet are already net of the provisions held against them, to the auditor's satisfaction.

P.label: Contingent liabilities
P.title: Off-balance-sheet exposures a bank must disclose
P.short: Claims, LC/BG, forward contracts, derivatives
P.law: Includes: claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts; liability on partly-paid investments; outstanding forward exchange/derivative contracts; guarantees (within/outside India); acceptances, endorsements and other obligations; other contingently-liable items; and bills for collection.
notes: Management representation should cover: all off-balance-sheet transactions are recorded when they occur, followed due process, are documented, and fully disclosed at year end; disclosed contingencies exclude any already-crystallised loss (which needs a provision instead); amounts are AS 29 best-estimates; directors' guarantees are backed by the party's own resources (s.20, BR Act compliance); remote-outcome items validly excluded with management's reasoning recorded.
Guarantee controls: sanctioned limits/margins adhered to; unused forms safeguarded; guarantee register marks expired guarantees; LC payments made strictly against conforming shipping documents.
Verify the forex 'net position' per currency is squared (or covered by a substantial amount) — an uncovered net position is an auditor query (RTP May 2025 Q16).

P.label: Statutory audit report
P.title: What the bank auditor's report must state
P.short: Nationalised-bank report to Central Govt + Rule 11 matters
P.law: For a nationalised bank, the auditor reports to the Central Government on: whether information/explanations called for were given and satisfactory; whether transactions coming to notice were within the bank's powers; whether branch/office returns were adequate for audit; whether the P&L shows a true balance of profit/loss; whether the balance sheet is full, fair and properly drawn to show a true and fair view; and any other matter the auditor thinks fit to raise. The report also complies with SA 700, 705, 706, 710 and 720, and must quantify (not just count) unaudited branches' advances, deposits, interest income and interest expense.
notes: CARO 2020 does not apply to a banking company (s.5(c), BR Act, 1949 definition) — a frequently tested negative point.

Rule 11, Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 matters the report must still cover: impact of pending litigation; provision for material foreseeable losses on long-term/derivative contracts; any delay in transferring amounts to the IEPF; the funds-advanced-to-intermediaries / funds-received-from-funding-parties representations (and whether anything contradicts them); compliance of dividend declared/paid with s.123, Companies Act, 2013; and the audit-trail (edit-log) feature requirement.

In addition to the s.143 Companies Act report, a banking company auditor is also required to state matters covered by s.143 itself (general reporting requirements) — this sits alongside, not instead of, the Central Government report for nationalised banks.

P.label: LFAR
P.title: The questionnaire-style report beyond the statutory report
P.short: Branch LFAR feeds the central LFAR, to RBI via the ACB
P.law: Beyond the statutory report, bank-auditor appointment terms require an LFAR — a questionnaire covering cash, balances with banks, investments, advances, deposits, etc. Both statutory branch auditors and SCAs give an LFAR; branch LFARs feed the SCA's consolidated bank-level LFAR.
notes: The bank-level LFAR, after examination, is placed before the Audit Committee of the Board (ACB) showing action taken/proposed on the irregularities raised; a copy (with the agenda note and Board's views/directions) goes to RBI within 60 days of the auditor's LFAR submission.
LFAR is where branch-level findings like title deeds held elsewhere, internal-control gaps on stationery, or unreconciled stock get specifically recorded.

P.label: Other SCA reports
P.title: Fraud reporting and the full list of SCA certificates
P.short: SA 240/250, s.143(12), and what else SCAs certify
P.law: SA 250 explains the duty of confidentiality is overridden by statute/law/courts; SA 240 makes the auditor responsible for reasonable assurance the FS are free of material misstatement from fraud or error. Under s.143(12), Companies Act, 2013, an auditor who has reason to believe a fraud of a prescribed amount is being/has been committed must report to the Central Government within the prescribed time/manner. The auditor need not examine every transaction — only evaluate the system as a whole — but an instance coming to notice in the ordinary course is reported to RBI in addition to the bank's Chairman/MD/CEO.
notes: Other certificates an SCA typically gives: adequacy/operating effectiveness of ICFR; LFAR; SLR compliance; treasury operations per RBI instructions; reconciliation of securities (own + PMS); compliance with key prudential/investment guidelines; IRAC compliance report; s.143(12) serious-irregularity report; custody/utilisation of unused BR forms; CRAR authentication; Ghosh Committee (frauds) / Jilani Committee (internal control) compliance status; adverse credit-deposit ratio in rural areas; asset-liability management; Corporate Governance certificate (listed banks); interest subsidy/subvention claims.

P.label: Concurrent audit — scope
P.title: What concurrent audit covers and why
P.short: Verification as the transaction happens, not pre-audit
P.law: Concurrent audit verifies transactions/activities as they take place — not a pre-audit — to catch deviations within the shortest possible time. It is akin to internal audit. The detailed scope is fixed uniformly for the bank by the Central Inspection and Audit Department in consultation with the ACB, with high-risk/high-value transactions prioritised over low-value ones.
notes: Broad coverage areas: cash, deposits, advances, investments, foreign exchange, housekeeping, and other items.

Foreign exchange procedures: foreign bills negotiated under LCs; FCNR/non-resident account debits-credits permissible under rules; inward/outward remittance accounting; forward-contract extension/cancellation authorisation and charge recovery; Nostro balances within prescribed limits; reasonableness of overbought/oversold position; adherence to RBI/HO dealing-room guidelines; Nostro/Vostro reconciliation.

Advances procedures: sanction within delegated authority; securities/documents received and properly charged/registered; post-disbursement follow-up; misutilisation/diversion check; LC/BG issuance within authority for genuine trade; overdue bill follow-up; RBI-compliant classification; timely DICGC/ECGC claims; prompt reporting/ratification of delegated-power breaches.

Housekeeping: proper ledger/register balancing incl. clean cash; timely reconciliation of inter-branch/suspense/sundry-deposit/DDRR/drafts accounts; percentage check of interest/discount/commission/exchange calculations; detection of revenue leakage through close scrutiny of income/expenditure.

P.label: CA auditor tenure
P.title: Tenure limits, remuneration and reporting lines
P.short: Max 5 years bank-wide, 3 years per branch
P.law: Banks choose between own staff (experienced, senior, independent of the audited branch) or external CA firms for concurrent audit. The ACB fixes the maximum tenure of an external concurrent auditor: generally not more than 5 years continuously with the bank, and not more than 3 years with any one branch/business unit.
notes: Serious acts of omission/commission by an external firm → appointment can be cancelled, reported to both RBI and ICAI.
Remuneration is fixed by the ACB based on area coverage, skill sets, staffing and time required.

Reporting: a structured format bank-wide; major deficiencies highlighted in a special note to the branch/controlling office immediately; a quarterly key-findings review to the ACB; zone-wise reporting plus an annual appraisal to the ACB; issues discussed with the branch manager before finalising the report; minor irregularities rectified promptly, serious ones escalated to HO; fraud detected is reported immediately to the Inspection & Audit Dept., the CVO and the branch manager (unless the branch manager is implicated).
P.mem: 5 years with the bank, 3 years with any one branch.

P.label: Audit committee
P.title: The ACB's oversight role
P.short: Directs and reviews the whole audit function
P.law: Banks constitute an Audit Committee of the Board (ACB) per RBI guidelines, which directs and oversees the bank's total audit function, reviews internal inspection/audit (system, quality, follow-up effectiveness), and reviews the appointment/remuneration/quality of concurrent auditors.
notes: The ACB's periodic meetings with concurrent and statutory auditors are how it actually exercises this oversight in practice.

P.label: Definition of NBFC
P.title: What makes a company an NBFC
P.short: The financial-assets / financial-income 50% test
P.law: s.45-I(f), RBI Act, 1934: an NBFC is (i) a financial institution which is a company, (ii) a non-banking company whose principal business is receiving deposits or lending in any manner, or (iii) any other non-banking institution/class RBI notifies. Principal business is decided by the principal-business criteria: a company is treated as an NBFC when, per its last audited balance sheet, its financial assets exceed 50% of total assets (net of intangible assets) AND its income from financial assets exceeds 50% of gross income. Both conditions must be met.
notes: Trap: satisfying only the asset test or only the income test is not enough — both must cross 50% (SM TYK Q3: Satyam Pvt Ltd fails because only the asset side qualifies).

Worked example: ABC Ltd — Financial assets ₹400.37cr (₹55.90cr non-current + ₹344.47cr current loans & advances) ÷ Total assets net of intangibles ₹527cr (₹530cr − ₹3cr) = 75.9%; Income from financial assets ₹52cr ÷ Gross income ₹102.57cr = 50.7%. Both >50% → qualifies as NBFC, can apply under s.45-IA (PYQ Dec 2021 Q4(c)).
P.mem: Financial assets/Total assets (net of intangibles) >50% AND Financial income/Gross income >50% — both, not either.

P.label: Registration & NOF
P.title: Section 45-IA registration and net owned fund
P.short: ₹10cr NOF glide path by 31.3.2027
P.law: s.45-IA, RBI Act, 1934: no NBFC may commence/carry on business without (a) a Certificate of Registration (CoR) from RBI, and (b) a Net Owned Fund (NOF) of the RBI-notified minimum. The general minimum NOF is being raised to ₹10 crore by 31 March 2027, phased (₹2cr → ₹5cr by 31.3.2025 → ₹10cr by 31.3.2027 for NBFC-ICC/MFI/Factors); NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA and NBFCs with no public funds/customer interface stay at ₹2 crore; NBFC-IFC and IDF-NBFC need ₹300 crore.
notes: Certain categories (regulated elsewhere, to avoid dual regulation) are exempt from registration: Housing Finance Institutions (NHB), Merchant Banking/Stock Exchanges/Stock-broking/Venture Capital Funds/AIFs (SEBI), Nidhi Companies (MCA), Insurance companies (IRDA), Chit Companies, specified Micro Finance Companies, Securitisation & Reconstruction Companies, Mutual Benefit Companies, and Core Investment Companies below ₹100cr assets (or ₹100cr+ not accessing public funds).

Auditor procedure where registration is missing/pending: examine RBI-Act-relevant transactions; check the 50%/50% principal-business test from the financials; check NOF against the requirement; if unregistered, document management's reasons; report under CARO 2020 cl.3(xvi)(a) whether registration was required and whether obtained.
P.upd:
NOF for most existing NBFC categories is on a glide path to ₹10 crore by 31 March 2027 — check which stage applies for the year under audit.

Check (not in the SM): RBI's 17 March 2022 notification lists the 31 March 2025 step as ₹5 crore for NBFC-ICC but ₹7 crore for NBFC-MFI (and, per the gazette text, ₹7 crore for NBFC-Factors; some summaries say ₹5 crore). The final ₹10 crore by 31 March 2027 is common to all three. The SM groups them; confirm before quoting the interim step.

P.label: Types of NBFCs
P.title: ICC, IFC, CIC, IDF-NBFC, MFI, Factors, NOFHC
P.short: Activity-based NBFC categories
P.law: By activity: Investment and Credit Company (ICC), Infrastructure Finance Company (IFC), Core Investment Company (CIC), Infrastructure Debt Fund-NBFC (IDF-NBFC), NBFC-Micro Finance Institution (MFI), NBFC-Factors, NOFHC (Non-Operative Financial Holding Company), and Asset Finance/Investment/Loan/Mortgage Guarantee Companies. Every NBFC is also either deposit-taking (NBFC-D) or non-deposit-taking (suffixed NBFC-ND).
notes: Deposit-taking NBFCs are always in the Middle Layer irrespective of asset size (see scale-based layers).

P.label: NBFC 4 layers
P.title: Base, Middle, Upper and Top Layer
P.short: Size, activity and perceived riskiness
P.law: RBI's Scale Based Regulation (effective 1 Oct 2022) sorts NBFCs into four layers: Base Layer (NBFC-BL) — non-deposit-taking NBFCs below ₹1,000 crore assets, plus NBFC-P2P/NBFC-AA/NOFHC/no-public-funds-no-customer-interface NBFCs; Middle Layer (NBFC-ML) — all deposit-taking NBFCs (any asset size), non-deposit NBFCs ≥₹1,000 crore, and Standalone Primary Dealers/IDF-NBFCs/CICs/HFCs/NBFC-IFCs; Upper Layer (NBFC-UL) — specifically identified by RBI on a scoring methodology (the top 10 NBFCs by asset size always sit here); Top Layer (NBFC-TL) — ideally empty, populated only if RBI sees substantial systemic-risk increase from an Upper Layer NBFC.
notes: NBFC-D, CIC, IFC, HFC sit in Middle or Upper Layer (never Base); SPD and IDF-NBFC always stay in Middle Layer; NBFC-P2P/AA/NOFHC/no-public-funds always stay in Base Layer; Government-owned NBFCs sit in Base or Middle Layer only (never Upper, until further notice); ICC/MFI/Factors/MGC can land in any layer depending on the scoring parameters.

From 1 Oct 2022: NBFC-ND = NBFC-BL; NBFC-D and NBFC-ND-SI = NBFC-ML or NBFC-UL as applicable (an NBFC-ND-SI between ₹500cr–₹1,000cr assets, unless otherwise mandated to Middle Layer, becomes NBFC-BL).
Common fact-pattern trap: a non-deposit-taking HFC/IFC with modest assets is still Middle Layer because of its activity, not Base Layer by size (SM TYU u2-2: Sugam Housing Finance, ₹800cr assets).
P.mem: Deposit-taking → always Middle (or Upper). Size alone only sorts non-deposit-taking, activity-less NBFCs.

P.label: NBFC vs bank
P.title: Four differences worth knowing cold
P.short: Demand deposits, PSS, DICGC, priority sector
P.law: (i) NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits (some can accept term deposits); (ii) NBFCs are not part of the payment and settlement system and cannot issue self-drawn cheques; (iii) DICGC deposit insurance is not available to NBFC depositors; (iv) NBFCs have no minimum priority-sector lending exposure requirement.
P.mem: No demand deposits, no PSS, no DICGC, no priority-sector floor.

P.label: NBFC capital norms
P.title: Minimum capital ratio, Tier I/II and risk weights
P.short: 15% total, Tier I ≥10% (12% for gold-loan NBFCs)
P.law: Every applicable NBFC must maintain a minimum capital ratio (Tier I + Tier II) of not less than 15% of aggregate risk-weighted assets (on- and off-balance-sheet). Tier I capital must be at least 10% at all times — except NBFCs primarily lending against gold jewellery (≥50% of financial assets), which must maintain Tier I ≥ 12%, now cross-referenced to the RBI (Lending Against Gold and Silver Collateral) Directions, 2025.
notes: Tier I (non-BL NBFCs) = Owned Fund, reduced by investments in shares/debentures/bonds/loans/deposits in subsidiaries & group companies exceeding 10% of owned fund in aggregate + perpetual debt instruments (capped at 15% of the prior year's aggregate Tier I). NBFC-BL cannot include perpetual debt instruments in Tier I (or Tier II) at all.

Tier II (non-BL NBFCs) = preference shares (other than compulsorily-convertible) + revaluation reserves (discounted 55%) + general/standard-asset provisions (up to 1.25% of RWA) + hybrid debt + subordinated debt + perpetual debt in excess of the Tier I cap — all capped so Tier II never exceeds Tier I.

Risk weights (selected): cash/bank balances/approved securities — 0%; PSU bank bonds — 20%; PFI FDs/CDs/bonds — 100%; shares/debentures/MF units of all companies — 100%; stock-on-hire/loans to staff/loans fully secured by own deposits — 0%; other secured loans/advances — 100% (retail consumer credit 125%, credit card receivables 125%); fixed assets (net) — 100%; Central-Government claims — 0%; State-Government-guaranteed claims not in default (or in default ≤90 days) — 20%; in default >90 days — 100%.

Worked example (PYQ Sep 2025 Q6): Easy Finance Ltd — cash/bank ₹8cr×0% + PFI bonds ₹50cr×100% + loans to staff ₹5cr×0% + furniture/fixtures ₹30cr×100% + State-Govt-guaranteed claims in default 75 days (≤90d) ₹60cr×20% = 0+50+0+30+12 = ₹92 crore aggregate risk-adjusted value.

Worked example — Tier I shortfall (PYQ May 2025 Q4(a)): Instant Finance Ltd (NBFC-BL, gold loans 60% of financial assets, RWA ₹1,000cr). Reported Tier I ₹130cr includes ₹15cr perpetual debt — excluded for an NBFC-BL → Tier I = ₹115cr. Required minimum (12% gold-loan floor) = 12%×₹1,000cr = ₹120cr. ₹115cr < ₹120cr → non-compliant. (An alternate working also nets off the >10%-of-owned-fund inter-NBFC investment, giving ₹113.33cr — still non-compliant.)
P.upd: Tier I definition for gold-loan NBFCs now explicitly ties to the RBI Gold Lending Directions, 2025 (compliance deadline 1 April 2026 has passed).
P.mem: CRAR 15% total, Tier I ≥10% (12% gold-loan NBFCs). Perpetual debt never counts for NBFC-BL.

P.label: NBFC income recognition
P.title: Realisation basis for NPA income
P.short: Same principle as banks
P.law: Income recognition follows recognised accounting principles; income (interest/discount/hire charges/lease rentals etc.) on an NPA is recognised only on actual realisation. Income recognised before the asset turned non-performing, if still unrealised, must be reversed.

P.label: NBFC classification
P.title: Standard / Sub-standard / Doubtful / Loss for NBFCs
P.short: 90-day NPA norm (glide path now complete)
P.law: Every applicable NBFC (except NBFC-MFIs) classifies lease/hire-purchase/loan assets into Standard, Sub-standard, Doubtful and Loss. NPA = overdue >90 days (interest, term-loan instalment, demand/call loan, bill, receivable, lease rental/HP instalment, or any linked facility to the same borrower, each per its own trigger). Classification is not upgraded merely by rescheduling unless the upgrade conditions are actually met.
notes: Sub-standard: NPA for ≤18 months (NBFC-BL) or ≤12 months for NBFC-ML and above; or an asset renegotiated/rescheduled/restructured, until 1 year of satisfactory performance on the new terms.
Doubtful: remains sub-standard beyond that same 18-month/12-month threshold.

Loss: identified as a loss by the NBFC/its auditor/RBI inspection (to the extent not written off), or adversely affected by non-recoverability (security-value erosion, no security, or fraud/omission by the borrower).

The 90-day NPA norm is the settled position for Nov 2026 — the SM's own glide path (>150 days by 31.3.2024 → >120 days by 31.3.2025 → >90 days by 31.3.2026) has run its course; don't describe it as still transitioning.

Worked example (PYQ Jan 2026 MCQ 8): SH Finance Ltd (Middle Layer), demand loan ₹3.8cr to RR Traders, NPA since 1 Sept 2023; realisable security value ₹2.2cr. By FY-end 31.3.2025 the NPA period (~19 months) exceeds the 12-month ML threshold → Doubtful (not merely Sub-standard).
P.upd: The NPA glide path to >90 days overdue is complete for Nov 2026 — treat it as the settled rule, not a transition.

P.label: NBFC provisioning
P.title: Provisioning percentages for sub-standard, doubtful and loss
P.law: Loss assets: written off entirely; if retained in the books for any reason, 100% of the outstanding is provided. Doubtful assets: 100% of the unsecured portion, plus a tiered % of the secured portion (realisable security value) by age as doubtful — 20% up to 1 year, 30% for 1–3 years, 50% beyond 3 years. Sub-standard assets: a flat 10% general provision on the total outstanding. Standard assets: 0.25% (NBFC-BL) / 0.40% (not applicable to NBFC-UL) of the outstanding, shown separately as 'Contingent Provisions against Standard Assets' — never netted from gross advances, and never reckoned in net-NPA arithmetic.
notes: Worked example (PYQ Jan 2026 MCQ 8, continued): RR Traders loan ₹3.8cr, realisable security ₹2.2cr → unsecured portion ₹1.6cr, provided 100% = ₹1.6cr. Doubtful since ~Sept 2024 (12-month ML cut from Sept 2023 NPA date); by 31.3.2025 that's <1 year doubtful → 20% of the ₹2.2cr secured portion = ₹0.44cr. Total provision = ₹1.6cr + ₹0.44cr = ₹2.04 crore.
P.mem: Loss 100% · Doubtful = 100% unsecured + 20/30/50% secured by age · Sub-standard 10% flat · Standard 0.25–0.40%.

P.label: NBFC audit procedure
P.title: Ascertaining the business, then testing compliance
P.short: MOA scan → internal control → registration → deposits → prudential norms
P.law: Steps: (1) scan the MOA/AOA and Board/committee minutes, corroborated against actual business done, to pin down the principal business activity — this drives classification and the public-deposit limits that follow; (2) evaluate the internal control system, especially the periodical-review system for advances (its absence risks undetected sticky advances); (3) verify registration u/s 45-IA and NOF compliance; (4) verify Public Deposit Directions compliance; (5) verify prudential-norms compliance.
notes: Public Deposit Directions checks: deposit ceiling linked to credit rating (and prompt NBFC action/RBI intimation on rating change; if rating falls below investment grade, an ICC/Factor must stop fresh deposits/renewals immediately, let existing deposits run off to maturity, and report to RBI within 15 working days); interest/brokerage/commission test-checked against specification; deposits accepted only on a proper written application with prescribed particulars; deposit register test-checked against receipts, and timely repayment (or reasons for delay) checked; approved liquid assets lodged in safe custody with a designated scheduled commercial bank, with an RBI certificate to that effect; returns filed timely; a Board resolution on file for NBFCs not accepting public deposits, or (for group holding investment companies) a resolution restricting investment to group shares/securities with no public deposits.

P.label: NBFC ICC checklist
P.title: Investments, loans and securities-lending checks
P.short: Illustrative checklist, not exhaustive
P.law: Physically verify shares/securities held (or a custodian/bank certificate); confirm no loan against the NBFC's own shares; dividend/interest income properly recognised (dividend on cash basis by default, accrual only if declared at AGM with right established; bond/debenture interest on accrual only if predetermined-rate and regularly serviced); board minutes support investment acquisitions/disposals and their current-vs-long-term classification; AS 13 compliance; depository confirmation for dematerialised holdings; securities-lending corporate-benefit pass-through verified; each loan/advance properly sanctioned, secured, documented; single/group borrower exposure limits respected; classification into Standard/Sub-standard/Doubtful/Loss and adequacy of provisioning checked.
notes: This list is illustrative, not exhaustive — the auditor tailors specific procedures to the NBFC's actual nature and size.

P.label: NBFC frauds
P.title: The 7 fraud categories and cash-shortage thresholds
P.short: IPC-based categories, reporting even without intent
P.law: Frauds are classified (mainly on IPC provisions) as: misappropriation/criminal breach of trust; fraudulent encashment via forged instruments/manipulated books/fictitious accounts; unauthorised credit facilities for reward/gratification; negligence and cash shortages; cheating and forgery; irregularities in forex transactions; any other type.
notes: 'Negligence/cash shortages' and 'forex irregularities' are reported as fraud only if intention to cheat is suspected/proved — except: cash shortages >₹10,000, or >₹5,000 if detected by management/auditor/inspecting officer and not reported on occurrence by the cash handler — these are reported as fraud regardless of proven intent.
NBFCs with overseas branches must report frauds there too, in the prescribed RBI format.
P.mem: ₹10,000 (any detection) · ₹5,000 (if caught by management/auditor/inspector, not self-reported).

P.label: Report to Board
P.title: The additional RBI-mandated report, beyond s.143
P.short: Matters A (all NBFCs) through D (CoR-exempt)
P.law: Under the NBFC Auditor's Report (RBI) Directions, 2016, every NBFC auditor files a separate report to the Board in addition to the s.143, Companies Act report. Matters cover: (A) all NBFCs — CoR obtained and still justified by the Principal Business Criteria as at year-end; NOF requirement met. (B) deposit-accepting NBFCs — additionally: public deposits within permissible limits; excess deposits regularised; credit rating in force and deposit ceiling respected; CRAR correctly determined and compliant; no violation of acceptance restrictions; no default to depositors; prudential-norms and liquid-assets compliance; timely RBI returns; branch opening/closure/agent-appointment compliance. (C) non-deposit-accepting NBFCs — Board resolution of non-acceptance passed; no deposits actually accepted; prudential-norms compliance; CRAR (Form NBS-7) correctly arrived at and filed timely; correct MFI classification if applicable. (D) CoR-exempt NBFCs — compliance with RBI's specific advised conditions.
notes: An unfavourable or qualified statement on any of these matters must state reasons; inability to opine must also state reasons.

A Statutory Auditor's Certificate (SAC) on CoR eligibility must separately reach RBI's regional DNBS office within 5 working days of signing the main audit report, but not later than 31 December of the same year.

P.label: Exception report to RBI
P.title: When the auditor must write to RBI directly
P.short: Unfavourable/qualified finding → report, don't certify compliance
P.law: If any matter in the Board report is unfavourable/qualified, or the auditor's opinion is that the NBFC hasn't complied with Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act, the Public Deposits Directions, or the Scale Based Regulation Directions, 2023, the auditor must send an exception report (with details) to the concerned Regional Office of DNBS having jurisdiction.
notes: The duty is limited to reporting contraventions only — the report must not contain any statement certifying compliance.

P.label: CARO 2020 for NBFCs
P.title: The NBFC-specific CARO clauses
P.short: cl.3(iii), 3(xvi) registration & CIC clauses
P.law: Clause 3(iii) (loans/guarantees/investments granted) requires reporting whether terms aren't prejudicial to the company, repayment schedules are stipulated and regular, the overdue->90-days total and recovery steps, and loans repayable on demand/without terms (incl. amounts to promoters/related parties). Clause 3(xvi): (a) whether registration u/s 45-IA was required and obtained; (b) whether the company conducted NBFC/HFC business without a valid CoR; (c) whether a Core Investment Company continues to meet CIC criteria (registered, exempted or unregistered); (d) the number of CICs in the Group, if more than one.

P.label: Ind AS applicability
P.title: Which NBFCs must comply with Ind AS
P.short: Rule 4(1)(iv), Companies (Ind AS) Rules, 2015
P.law: NBFCs are brought into Ind AS by Rule 4(1)(iv) of the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, as amended by the 2023 Amendment Rules.

P.label: Division III format
P.title: Balance sheet and P&L for Ind-AS NBFCs
P.short: MCA notification, 11 Oct 2018
P.law: NBFCs complying with Ind AS present FS under Division III, Schedule III, Companies Act, 2013 (MCA notification, 11 October 2018). The balance sheet splits assets into Financial Assets (cash equivalents, bank balance, derivatives, receivables, loans, investments, other financial assets) and Non-Financial Assets (inventories, tax assets, PPE, intangibles, etc.); liabilities into Financial Liabilities (derivatives, payables, debt securities, borrowings, deposits, subordinated liabilities) and Non-Financial Liabilities. The P&L separately shows Revenue from Operations (interest, dividend, rental, fee/commission income, fair-value gains, etc.) before Other Income.

P.label: Div II vs III
P.title: Six differences from the non-NBFC Ind AS format
P.short: Liquidity order, 1% disclosure, LLP debts, OCI on face
P.law: Division III (NBFCs) differs from Division II (non-NBFC Ind-AS companies): (a) NBFCs may present the balance sheet in order of liquidity (not allowed under Division II); (b) NBFCs separately disclose any 'other income'/'other expenditure' item exceeding 1% of total income (Division II: 1% of revenue from operations or ₹10 lakh, whichever is higher); (c) NBFCs separately disclose, under receivables, debts due from any LLP in which its director is a partner/member; (d) NBFCs show 'revenue from operations' and 'other comprehensive income' on the face of the P&L, not only in notes; (e) separate disclosure of trade receivables with significant credit-risk increase / credit-impaired; (f) statutory-reserve distribution conditions/restrictions separately disclosed in notes.
notes: Worked check: 'other expenditure' only needs separate disclosure once it exceeds 1% of total income — e.g. manpower outsourcing cost ₹99.50cr against total income ₹10,000cr is 0.995%, just under the line, so no separate disclosure is required (SM TYU u2-3).

P.label: Exam scope — Nov 2026
P.title: What's current for Nov 2026 that the printed SM doesn't say
P.short: RTP May 2026 statutory update, in one place
P.law: Three points from ICAI's own RTP academic update, none of which the printed SM text states: (1) NBFC-MFI must keep ≥60% of total assets (net of intangibles) in microfinance loans on an ongoing basis (RBI circular, 6 June 2025); failing this for 4 consecutive quarters means approaching RBI with a remediation plan. (2) Gold-loan NBFC Tier 1 (≥50% financial assets in gold loans, 12% floor) now explicitly follows the RBI (Lending Against Gold and Silver Collateral) Directions, 2025 for on-/off-balance-sheet treatment; compliance was due by 1 April 2026 — that date has passed, so treat it as settled, not pending. (3) The risk-weighted-assets table's 'Others (to be specified)' line now explicitly includes ROU assets (₹, 100% weight).
notes: A fourth point worth knowing even though it isn't a change: the NBFC NPA glide path to >90 days is now complete (SM's own schedule ran to 31.3.2026) — don't describe it as transitional in an answer for this attempt.

P.label: Beyond: MFI 60% test
P.title: What counts as a 'microfinance loan' for the 60% test
P.short: RBI Microfinance Loans Directions, 2022
P.law: The RBI (Regulatory Framework for Microfinance Loans) Directions, 2022 define a microfinance loan broadly as a collateral-free loan to a low-income household (annual household income up to a notified ceiling), used to gauge whether an NBFC-MFI's book is genuinely microfinance-led. The exact income ceiling and detailed eligibility conditions are a regulatory figure that must be checked against the current RBI Master Direction before quoting a number in an answer.
notes: Concept-based exam angle: an NBFC-MFI whose microfinance book slips under 60% isn't instantly deregistered — it gets a remediation window, but four straight quarters of shortfall forces RBI engagement.

P.label: Beyond: RBIA
P.title: What a Risk-Based Internal Audit actually assesses
P.short: Business risk × control risk → residual risk matrix
P.law: RBIA (SM §4.2) is only sketched in the printed material. Conceptually, RBIA evaluates inherent business risk (nature of the branch's activity) against the effectiveness of controls mitigating it, to derive a residual/control risk rating per branch, which then drives audit frequency and depth (a high-risk branch gets audited more often/deeply than a low-risk one) — the same logic SA 315 uses for engagement-level risk assessment, applied bank-wide as a planning tool.
notes: Exam angle: expect a fact pattern describing branch characteristics (volume, product mix, past irregularities) and asking you to say whether RBIA frequency/depth is justified — reason from the risk-matrix logic, not a memorised number.

P.label: Beyond: SARFAESI
P.title: Recovery without going to court first
P.short: Listed in the legal framework, never elaborated
P.law: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 lets a secured creditor (bank/NBFC meeting the eligibility threshold) take possession of and sell secured assets after a defaulting borrower (classified NPA) fails to repay within 60 days of a demand notice, without first obtaining a civil-court decree. It works alongside — not instead of — the NPA classification/provisioning rules already in the SM: SARFAESI is a recovery remedy once an account is already NPA.
notes: Exam angle: a question could ask why a bank chose SARFAESI over a civil suit, or what happens to NPA classification/provisioning while SARFAESI proceedings are pending (classification doesn't pause merely because recovery action has started).

P.label: Beyond: priority sector
P.title: Why 'priority sector' classification matters to the auditor
P.short: Sectoral disclosure the SM mentions but doesn't define
P.law: The SM notes advances are classified sectorally (priority vs public sector) but doesn't define priority sector. Conceptually: RBI mandates banks to direct a target share of adjusted net bank credit toward priority sectors (agriculture, MSME, export credit, housing, education, social infrastructure, renewable energy, etc.) — shortfalls are funded into RIDF-type funds. The auditor's angle is verifying the sectoral classification used for the disclosure and the PSL-achievement certificate is correctly tagged, not computing the target itself (which is a regulatory figure to check, not memorise).

P.label: Beyond: co-op banks
P.title: What's different when the entity is a co-operative bank
P.short: Dual regulation — Registrar + RBI
P.law: Co-operative banks sit under dual regulation: incorporation/registration and day-to-day governance under the (State) Co-operative Societies Act, 1912/State Acts, while banking-business prudential norms (CRR/SLR, licensing, NPA/provisioning, capital adequacy) come from the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (as applicable to co-operative banks) and RBI directions. The statutory auditor is typically appointed under the co-operative statute/Registrar's process rather than a shareholders' AGM, and an additional report may go to the Registrar of Co-operative Societies alongside the usual bank-audit reporting.
notes: Exam angle: a concept-based question could ask you to spot that a co-operative bank's auditor answers to two regulators, not one, and that appointment/removal follows the co-operative statute, not s.139–140 Companies Act machinery.

Q.q: CA Harshit is conducting the statutory audit of a branch of a public sector bank. On examining 20 large advances, he finds that in 5 cases loan applications were filled incompletely with important details left out, and cash credit limits were enhanced during the year with no record of assessment of the enhanced working capital requirement in the borrower files or system. However, all five accounts are operating satisfactorily and are classified as standard assets. Would this information prompt the auditor to suggest a change in asset classification? What does the situation reflect?
Q.a:
Classification: an account becomes NPA when it ceases to generate income for the bank. Here all five accounts operate satisfactorily, so there is no reason to suggest a change in classification — they remain Standard.

What it reflects: the incomplete loan applications and absence of any record assessing the enhanced working-capital requirement show that internal control over advances at the branch is not proper — a deficiency in credit appraisal.

Conclusion: such deficiencies need to be highlighted by the auditor in the LFAR, even though classification itself doesn't change.
Q.trap: Concluding the accounts must be downgraded because paperwork is missing — classification follows actual performance (income generation), not documentation quality; the documentation gap is an LFAR control point, not an NPA trigger.

Q.q: You are the concurrent auditor of a large public sector bank branch with advances of about ₹500 crore, including export advances of ₹300 crore. Some borrowers also get LCs issued by the branch for importing raw diamonds from Belgium. Focusing on advances, discuss any five areas you would verify to ensure there is no revenue leakage.
Q.a:
Five revenue-leakage checks on advances:

(i) Interest rates fed into the system verified against the corresponding sanction letters, to ensure correct application at the stipulated intervals.

(ii) Processing fees on fresh/renewed advances levied as per bank guidelines, and any revision given effect to per circulars.

(iii) Non-submission of stock statements (a condition of CC sanction) correctly attracts penal interest — verify this is levied.

(iv) Overdue interest on export bills purchased/packing credit for the overdue period is correctly charged.

(v) Charges/commission on LCs issued (the diamond-import LCs here) are levied per the bank's circulars/manual.
Q.trap: Treating this as a generic internal-control-over-advances answer — the ask is specifically revenue leakage, so the answer must stay on fee/interest/charge computation points, not documentation/sanction-authority points.

Q.q: CA Seema, appointed stock auditor of Bhawani Rice Mills Pvt. Ltd. (cash credit limit ₹12 crore against paid stocks and debtors up to 90 days, margin 25%), visits the premises and test-checks quantity of paddy (20,000 quintals) and rice (8,000 bags). She computes drawing power of ₹12.05 crore and submits her report. A week later, the bank's regular internal inspector finds that about 5,000 bags of rice (value ≈ ₹1.50 crore) were fungus-ridden and had been held for 15 months. How do you view the situation?
Q.a:
View: the stock auditor's work was not performed diligently. Verifying physical quantities on a test-check basis is not the limit of a stock auditor's role — condition/quality of the stock also had to be checked, since damaged/unsellable stock cannot support drawing power.

What she should have done: opened bags on a test-check basis, which would have revealed the fungus-ridden condition; the value of such rice should then have been excluded from stock value when computing drawing power.

Conclusion: CA Seema failed to perform her work diligently, and the drawing power of ₹12.05 crore reported to the bank is incorrect (overstated).
Q.trap: Assuming a quantity test-check is sufficient for a stock audit — value depends on saleable condition, not just physical presence, and 15 months' holding of rice should itself have raised suspicion.

Q.q: Your firm is Central Statutory Auditor of a nationalised bank (financial year = accounting year). The Audit Manager reports that the bank recognised, on accrual basis, income from dividends on securities and Units of Mutual Funds held by it at year end — but the dividends were declared only after the financial year ended. Comment.
Q.a:
Rule: banks may book dividend income on shares of corporate bodies on an accrual basis only if the dividend has been declared by the corporate body at its AGM and the owner's right to receive payment is established — consistent with AS 9. For government securities and corporate bonds/debentures with a pre-determined interest rate, income may be accrued provided interest is serviced regularly (not in arrears); banks may also accrue income on securities of bodies whose interest/principal is centrally/state-government guaranteed.

Analysis: here the dividend was declared after the financial year end.

Conclusion: recognising this dividend on an accrual basis is not in order.
Q.trap: Treating all investment income as accrual-eligible — dividend income specifically needs the AGM declaration to have already happened within the year; interest income has a separate (regularity-of-servicing) test.

Q.q: As statutory central auditors of a nationalised bank, what special points should you bear in mind when auditing compliance with Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements?
Q.a: Key points for SLR audit: obtain an understanding of the RBI circulars governing DTL composition; request branch auditors to send weekly Friday trial balances (consolidated at HO to fix the DTL position each reporting Friday) and specifically verify branch cash balances on the selected dates; test-check the HO's consolidation of DTL against branch returns, and whether securities are valued per RBI guidelines; specifically examine the exclusion/inclusion items prescribed by RBI when computing DTL; examine whether Form A (CRR) and Form VIII (SLR) return data is correct on a sample basis; verify compliance is reported for 12 odd dates in different months, none a Friday; and consider the auditor's responsibility around Automated Data Flow (ADF) reporting.
Q.trap: Describing SLR as simply "a liquidity ratio to check" without naming the DTL-computation mechanics — that's exactly where the marks sit.

Q.q: Explain the scope of concurrent audit of a bank with reference to RBI guidelines.
Q.a:
