Scope: determined uniformly for the bank as a whole by the Central Inspection and Audit Department, in consultation with the Audit Committee of the Board (ACB), with priority given to high-risk/high-value transactions over lower-value ones. RBI's guidelines cover all key activity areas at the branch under audit — broadly cash, deposits, advances, investments, foreign exchange and housekeeping, with most banks running their own detailed Audit Manual.

The system is part of the bank's early-warning mechanism for timely detection of irregularities/lapses and fraud prevention; management must give serious attention to branch/coverage selection, auditor appointment, reporting procedures and follow-up, and review the system's effectiveness at least once a year.
Q.trap: Listing only the six coverage areas without explaining why concurrent audit exists (early-warning, fraud prevention) — ICAI's answer always frames scope around that purpose.

Q.q: During the audit of Good Samaritan Bank as at 31 March 2024, you observe: (a) an account with no recovery for the past 18 months, where the bank has not applied NPA/income-recognition norms because the advance is guaranteed by the Central Government (guarantee not invoked) — please respond, and would your answer differ if guaranteed by a State Government instead? (b) the advance portfolio includes significant loans against Life Insurance Policies — write a suitable audit programme to verify these.
Q.a:
(a) Government-guaranteed advance: if a government-guaranteed advance becomes NPA, interest should not be taken to income unless realised, regardless of the guarantee — but for asset classification, a Central-Government-guaranteed credit facility is treated as NPA only once the guarantee is invoked and repudiated. Since the bank hasn't invoked the guarantee, it is correct not to apply NPA norms for provisioning purposes — but this carve-out doesn't extend to income recognition, so unrecovered income must be reversed. If instead State-Government guaranteed: this exception does not apply — the advance must be treated as NPA once it is overdue for more than 90 days, guarantee or not.

(b) Audit programme for LIP-backed advances: inspect the policies for assignment to the bank, registered with the insurer; verify premiums are paid and policies in force; examine the insurer's surrender-value certificate; where surrender value is subject to a premium payment, confirm that premium has been deducted from the surrender value.
Q.trap: Applying the Central-Government carve-out to a State-Government guarantee — the SM is explicit that the exception is Central-Government only.

Q.q: As Central Statutory Auditors of a nationalised bank, you find the bank is a consortium member of a ₹50 crore cash-credit facility to X Ltd (bank's own share ₹10 crore). Over the last two quarters, against a debit of ₹1.75 crore towards interest, credits in X Ltd's account total only ₹1.25 crore. Based on the lead bank's certificate, the bank has classified X Ltd's account as performing. Advise.
Q.a:
Rule: in a consortium, each bank classifies the advance given by it per its own experience of recovery and other factors — a lead bank's certificate doesn't bind member banks' classification.

Analysis: interest debited over the last two quarters (₹1.75cr) exceeds credits received (₹1.25cr) by ₹0.50cr — the amount remains outstanding.

Conclusion: the interest already credited to income must be reversed, and the account shown as a non-performing asset, despite the lead bank's certificate that it is performing.
Q.trap: Deferring to the lead bank's classification — consortium member banks classify independently.

Q.q: LCO Bank, a nationalized bank, provides credit card facilities. How will you evaluate the internal control system in the area of credit card operations?
Q.a: Evaluate for: effective screening of applications with sound credit assessment; strict control over storage/issue of cards; a system for merchants to confirm unutilised limit before accepting settlement above a specified % of the cardholder's limit; prompt merchant reporting of accepted settlements; reimbursement to merchants only after verifying validity, charged gross of commission immediately to the customer's account; regular/prompt statements to customers; monitoring and follow-up of payments; prompt identification of overdue payments and credit-stop action via merchant bulletins for defaulters; periodic review of cardholder accounts, including determination of doubtful amounts and their provisioning.
Q.trap: Stopping at "control over storage and issue of cards" — that's only one of eight control points ICAI expects.

Q.q: You are Concurrent Auditor of a nationalized bank branch whose main business is dealing in foreign exchange. Suggest the main areas of coverage with regard to foreign exchange transactions under concurrent audit.
Q.a:
Coverage areas: foreign bills negotiated under letters of credit; FCNR and other non-resident accounts — debits/credits permissible under the rules; inward/outward remittances properly accounted for; extension/cancellation of forward contracts, duly authorised with charges recovered; Nostro-account balances in different currencies within prescribed limits; overbought/oversold position reasonable for the scale of operations; adherence to RBI/HO guidelines on dealing-room operations; verification/reconciliation of Nostro and Vostro account transactions/balances.

Also asked (ICAI): PYQ December 2021 · Q3(b) (re-dated, 'Coin Bank Ltd').
Q.trap: Confusing Nostro (our account with a foreign bank) with Vostro (a foreign bank's account with us) when writing the reconciliation point.

Q.q: While auditing FAIR Bank, you observe that a lump-sum amount has been disclosed as contingent liability collectively. Management asks you to guide them about the disclosure requirement for contingent liabilities of banks.
Q.a:
Rule: contingent liabilities must be disclosed item-wise, not as a single lump sum — the Third Schedule requires separate disclosure of: claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts; liability on partly-paid investments; liability on outstanding forward exchange and derivative contracts; guarantees given on behalf of constituents (within/outside India); acceptances, endorsements and other obligations; and other items for which the bank is contingently liable (e.g. underwriting contracts, bills rediscounting, disputed tax demands) — plus bills for collection shown separately.

Conclusion: the bank's collective lump-sum disclosure does not meet the Schedule's item-wise disclosure requirement and should be corrected.
Q.trap: Treating "contingent liability" as a single catch-all line — the Schedule wants each category broken out.

Q.q: ABC Chartered Accountants are concurrent auditors for the branches of Effective Bank Ltd for 2023-24. You are on the Agra-branch team and instructed by your senior to verify advances for the audit period. Guide your assistant on the areas to cover while verifying advances in a concurrent audit.
Q.a: Verification areas: loans/advances sanctioned in accordance with delegated authority; securities and documents received and properly charged/registered; post-disbursement supervision/follow-up proper (stock statements, instalments, recovery/renewal); no misutilisation or diversion of funds; LCs issued within delegated power and for genuine trade transactions; bank guarantees properly worded, recorded in the register and renewed on time; overdue bills of exchange properly followed up; classification of advances per RBI guidelines; DICGC/ECGC claims submitted in time; instances of exceeding delegated powers promptly reported to and confirmed/ratified by controlling office/HO.
Q.trap: Writing a generic "check the file" answer instead of naming the specific ten-point checklist ICAI expects for concurrent-audit advances verification.

Q.q: During the audit of Skip Bank Ltd, you find the bank sold certain of its non-performing assets. Draft the audit-check points relevant to this area.
Q.a: Audit-check points on NPA sale: Board policy on procedure, valuation and delegation of powers for such sales is followed; only an NPA that has remained NPA in the bank's books for at least 2 years is sold; the asset is sold without recourse (entire credit risk transfers to the buyer); the bank assumes no legal/operational/other residual risk after sale; the sale is on a cash basis only, never at a contingent price, with the entire consideration received upfront; the bank has not bought back an NPA it originally sold; on sale, the asset is removed from the selling bank's books; if sold below net book value, the shortfall is debited to that year's P&L; if sold above net book value, the excess is not recognised as profit and the excess provision is not reversed — it is retained to meet shortfall/loss on sale of other NPAs.
Q.trap: Allowing profit recognition on a sale above NBV — ICAI's answer is emphatic that this is never booked as profit.

Q.q: Banks, because of certain characteristics, are distinguished from other commercial enterprises and hence need special audit consideration. As an auditor, specify the peculiarities that necessitate this.
Q.a: Peculiarities driving special audit consideration: custody of large volumes of cash/negotiable instruments (vulnerable to misappropriation, needing rigorous internal control); large volume/variety of transactions requiring complex, heavily IT-dependent accounting and control systems; a wide network of geographically dispersed branches with decentralised authority (uniform practice/accounting difficult, more so across national boundaries); significant commitments assumed without fund transfer (off-balance-sheet items, where failure to record may go undetected); transactions initiated at one location, recorded at another, managed at a third; transactions directly initiated and completed by the customer alone (ATM/internet/mobile) without bank-employee intervention; international settlement-system linkages posing systemic risk; and regulatory requirements that often shape accounting/auditing practice itself.
Q.trap: Listing only 2–3 points — ICAI's own answer runs to eight, and partial answers lose marks proportionally.

Q.q: ABC Bank sanctioned credit limits of ₹100 lakh to M/s Volkart Ltd on 1 Sept 2021; renewal was due 1 Sept 2023. During the statutory branch audit for the year ended 31 March 2024, you find the renewal has not been done despite 180 days being over, though the renewal process was initiated on time, most documents received, and the account operates regularly within drawing power. A letter from Volkart explains the delay (new auditor due to the prior auditor's sudden death); audited financials were received on 10 April 2024 and the renewal letter issued immediately thereafter. Your assistant insists the account must be classified NPA since the limit wasn't renewed as at 31 March 2024. What is your opinion?
Q.a:
Rule: per RBI guidelines, an account should be classified NPA if the regular/ad hoc limit is not reviewed within 180 days of the due date.

Analysis: here operations are excellent, the delay is genuinely explained (auditor's death), and critically the renewal was issued before the audit report was signed — this makes it an adjusting event under AS 4, Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date, relating back to the position as at the balance-sheet date; it is also a matter of substance over form.

Conclusion: the account should be classified as a Standard asset, not NPA — the assistant's view is incorrect.
Q.trap: Applying the 180-day rule mechanically without checking whether a post-balance-sheet-date renewal (issued before the audit report is signed) is an AS 4 adjusting event.

Q.q: At a small bank branch (manager, cashier, and staff S1/S2/S3), S1 (a peon) opens all mail and forwards it, without a signature book to check signatures on important communications. S2 holds all bank forms (cheque books, DD/pay-order books, traveller's cheques, forex cards) and maintains a meticulous record you have test-checked — but no one regularly checks it. The bank says a small branch with staff shortage cannot always check the work and records. Comment.
Q.a:
Violations of general internal control: mail should be opened by a responsible officer, with signatures on letters/advices from other branches checked against the signature book — a peon with no signature book opening all mail breaches this. Bank forms must be kept in the possession of an officer, and another responsible officer must verify the issuance and stock of such stationery — S2's own meticulous record-keeping doesn't substitute for independent verification by someone else.

On the bank's defence: staff shortage does not excuse these lapses — they pose a real risk of fraud regardless of branch size.

Conclusion: the auditor should report these internal-control deficiencies.
Q.trap: Accepting "small branch, limited staff" as a valid excuse — ICAI's answer explicitly rejects that reasoning.

Q.q: NRF Bank Ltd, suffering from a high NPA count, decides in April 2024 (for the first time) to sell NPAs. The proposed accounts: Fin Pvt. Ltd. (NPA since FY 2020-21, ₹36.55L); Dairy Works (NPA since FY 2022-23, ₹55.24L); Book Store (NPA since FY 2019-20, ₹29.85L); Fancy Corp. (NPA since FY 2018-19, ₹61.42L); RSM and Associates (NPA since FY 2021-22, ₹19.25L). As internal auditor, scrutinize the proposal and advise which accounts can be sold.
Q.a:
Rule: only an NPA that has remained NPA in the bank's books for at least 2 years may be sold (counted from the NPA financial year to April 2024, i.e. the cut-off is FY 2021-22 or earlier).

Analysis: Fin Pvt. Ltd. (2020-21), Book Store (2019-20), Fancy Corp. (2018-19) and RSM and Associates (2021-22) have all been NPA for 2 years or more by April 2024. Dairy Works (2022-23) has been NPA for under 2 years as of April 2024.

Total sellable: ₹36.55L + ₹29.85L + ₹61.42L + ₹19.25L = ₹147.07 lakh. Conclusion: NRF Bank can sell all five NPAs except Dairy Works (₹55.24 lakh), which does not yet meet the 2-year holding test.
Q.trap: Forgetting that the 2-year test is measured against the NPA's financial year of origin, not the calendar date of the oldest entry — Dairy Works (2022-23) is the one to exclude, not RSM (2021-22).
nums: Total NPA amount that can be sold

Q.q: PDSJ & Associates, statutory auditors of a scheduled commercial bank for 2023-24, find that term-loan borrower accounts are classified into SMA/NPA as follows in the system: an account becomes overdue on the very next day after a missed due date (e.g. due 31 March 2023, unpaid → overdue 1 April 2023); it is tagged SMA-1 on 1 May 2023 if it continues overdue; SMA-2 on 31 May 2023; and NPA on 30 June 2023 if it remains overdue even after SMA-2. Evaluate this control design for regulatory compliance.
Q.a:
Rule: any amount due under a credit facility is 'overdue' if unpaid on the due date fixed by the bank — accounts are flagged overdue as part of the day-end process for that very date, not the next day. SMA/NPA classification date is the calendar date on which the day-end process classifying that status is run — so SMA-1 falls due on completion of 30 continuous overdue days, SMA-2 on 60 days, NPA on completion of 90 days (as applicable), each measured from the actual overdue date.

Analysis: the bank's design pushes the overdue date to the next calendar day (1 April instead of 31 March) — this delays every subsequent SMA/NPA tagging date by one day each time (SMA-1 should be 30 April 2023, not 1 May; SMA-2 should be 30 May, not 31 May; NPA should be 29 June, not 30 June).

Conclusion: the control design is not in accordance with RBI's regulatory guidelines — overdue status must be fixed as at the due date itself, and all downstream dates recalculated from there.
Q.trap: Accepting the bank's "next-day" logic as harmless rounding — each misdated trigger compounds, systematically delaying every classification by one day.

Q.q: RML & Associates, joint auditors of IND Bank for 2023-24, are analysing industry NPA data for risk assessment: BIC Bank — Gross NPA ₹55,000cr, Net NPA ₹13,000cr, Net NPA/Net Advances 1.72%; ABD Bank — ₹45,000cr / ₹10,000cr / 2.34%; RIN Bank — ₹55,000cr / ₹18,000cr / 2.65%; IND Bank — ₹28,000cr / ₹6,500cr / 3.97%; CRB Bank — ₹35,000cr / ₹8,800cr / 2.27%. What are 'Gross NPAs' and 'Net NPAs', and what inference follows from comparing IND Bank's ratio to the others?
Q.a:
Gross NPAs: opening NPA balance, increased by fresh NPAs during the year, reduced by upgradations/recoveries/write-offs during the year.

Net NPAs: Gross NPAs less the total provision held against NPAs, less balance in the interest-suspense account parking accrued-but-unrealised NPA interest, less certain other adjustments.

Inference: IND Bank's Net NPA/Net Advances ratio (3.97%) is the highest among the peer set — this signals a risk that IND Bank may not have made adequate provisions per RBI guidelines; a higher ratio indicates a higher probability/risk of under-provisioning, so the auditor should tailor audit procedures to specifically examine and verify this area for IND Bank.
Q.trap: Treating the ratio purely as a performance metric — as auditor the inference to draw is specifically about provisioning adequacy risk, not just asset quality.

Q.q: CA J, statutory auditor of a nationalized bank branch, is focusing on verification of Current Accounts & Savings Accounts (CASA) maintained at the branch. Suggest a few audit procedures he should follow.
Q.a: CASA audit procedures: on a sample basis, verify current/savings accounts opened during the year for KYC-norm adherence; confirm savings accounts are opened only for individuals/HUF/approved institutions (never for business/professional concerns, which use current accounts); verify balances in individual accounts on a sample basis; test-check interest calculations (noting current accounts generally carry no interest); check the periodic balance-confirmation procedure is followed consistently, sampling confirmations received; ensure debit balances in current accounts are not netted against liabilities but shown under 'advances'; specifically examine inoperative/dormant accounts (no transactions for over 2 years) revived/closed during the year, checking proper authority for revival and for any account with a significant balance reduction vs. the prior year.
Q.trap: Forgetting the 2-year inoperative-account rule — it's the fraud-risk point examiners specifically probe for CASA questions.

Q.q: 'Fin Crazy' is a P2P online platform owned by Future Technologies Pvt. Ltd, registered with RBI as an NBFC-P2P (loan facilitation intermediary — connecting lenders/borrowers, carrying out credit assessment/risk profiling, loan documentation and recovery services). It falls outside the Upper Layer. Where does this NBFC fit under scale-based regulation? Suggest a few audit procedures for it.
Q.a:
Layer: NBFC-P2P platforms always sit in the Base Layer under scale-based regulation, regardless of size.

Audit procedures: understand the business — confirm the company undertakes only activities permissible to an NBFC-P2P (an online marketplace connecting lenders/borrowers) and is not lending on its own account; verify the RBI certificate of registration for the P2P platform; verify the Board-approved policy on participant (lender/borrower) eligibility; verify the Board-approved pricing policy for platform services; verify adherence to RBI lending/borrowing guidelines for P2P platforms; verify proper arrangements are in place among participants and the NBFC-P2P; check compliance with RBI reporting requirements; verify a Board-approved grievance-redressal/complaints policy.
Q.trap: Classifying by asset size — NBFC-P2P (like NBFC-AA/NOFHC/no-public-funds NBFCs) is one of the categories placed in the Base Layer by activity, irrespective of size.

Q.q: Sugam Housing Finance Limited, asset size ₹800 crore, is principally engaged in providing housing finance mainly to individuals and is not identified by RBI in the Upper Layer. Under scale-based regulations, what is the appropriate classification? Is there a specific CARO 2020 reporting requirement for a housing-finance-activity auditor?
Q.a:
Classification: since Housing Finance Companies always sit in the Middle Layer or Upper Layer (never Base) by activity — asset size is irrelevant here. As Sugam is not RBI-identified for the Upper Layer, it falls in the Middle Layer.

CARO 2020: Clause 3(xvi)(b) specifically requires the auditor to report whether the company has conducted any non-banking financial or housing finance activity without a valid Certificate of Registration (CoR) from RBI under the RBI Act, 1934.
Q.trap: Reasoning from the ₹1,000 crore Base/Middle asset-size threshold — that threshold only sorts plain non-deposit NBFCs; HFCs are Middle/Upper by activity regardless of size.

Q.q: You audit a deposit-taking NBFC (NBFC-D) identified by RBI in the Upper Layer, preparing FS under Ind AS (Division III, Schedule III). An extract of its P&L for the year ended 31 March 2024 (₹ crore, previous year ignored): Interest income 9,500; Rental income 150; Fees & commission income 100; Net gain on fair value changes 150 → Total revenue from operations 9,900; Other income 100; Total income 10,000. 'Other expenditure' includes manpower outsourcing cost of ₹99.50 crore. Does this meet the Division III disclosure requirement?
Q.a:
Rule: under Division III, an NBFC must separately disclose by way of a note any item of 'other income' or 'other expenditure' exceeding 1% of total income.

Computation: 1% of Total Income (₹10,000 crore) = ₹100 crore. The manpower outsourcing cost is ₹99.50 crore, which is below ₹100 crore.

Conclusion: the expenditure does not exceed 1% of total income — the requirement for separate disclosure by way of a note is therefore met (i.e., no separate note is required, and the company's treatment is compliant).
Q.trap: Comparing ₹99.50cr against 1% of revenue from operations (₹9,900cr → ₹99cr), which is the Division II test, not Division III's — Division III's threshold is 1% of total income, not revenue from operations.

Q.q: Define NBFC. Also give a brief description of the types of NBFCs, covering any five.
Q.a:
Definition (s.45-I(f), RBI Act, 1934): (i) a financial institution which is a company; (ii) a non-banking company whose principal business is receiving deposits (in any manner) or lending (in any manner); (iii) any other non-banking institution/class RBI notifies with Central Government approval.

Five types: ICC (Investment and Credit Company) — general lending/investment NBFC; IFC (Infrastructure Finance Company) — deploys the bulk of assets in infrastructure loans; CIC (Core Investment Company) — holds equity/debt mainly in group companies; IDF-NBFC — refinances infrastructure projects via bonds; NBFC-MFI — predominantly microfinance lending to low-income households.
Q.trap: Giving generic descriptions without naming the regulatory abbreviation ICAI expects (ICC/IFC/CIC/IDF-NBFC/MFI etc.) — the examiner is checking you know the vocabulary, not just the concept.

Q.q: Shubham & Associates are starting the audit of NBFCs, having done little such work before. Explain the registration and regulation requirements an auditor needs to keep in mind while planning an NBFC audit.
Q.a: Requirements to keep in mind: under s.45-IA, RBI Act, 1934, no NBFC may commence/carry on business without (a) a Certificate of Registration from RBI and (b) the RBI-notified minimum Net Owned Fund (originally ₹25 lakh, raised to ₹2 crore for CoR granted on/after 21 April 1999, with several categories now on a glide path to ₹10 crore). Certain categories regulated elsewhere are exempt from RBI registration to avoid dual regulation — Venture Capital/Merchant Banking/Stock-broking companies and Stock Exchanges (SEBI), Insurance companies (IRDA), Nidhi Companies (s.406, Companies Act, 2013), Chit Companies (Chit Funds Act, 1982), and Housing Finance Companies (NHB). RBI has also issued directions on public-deposit acceptance, prudential norms (capital adequacy, income recognition, asset classification, provisioning, risk exposure) and reporting — and separately, directions requiring auditors to report non-compliance to RBI, the Board and shareholders.
Q.trap: Assuming every finance company must register with RBI — the exemption list (SEBI/IRDA/MCA/NHB-regulated entities) is exactly what a newly-onboarding firm needs to check first.

Q.q: Satyam Pvt Ltd is engaged in trading activities, and has also made investments in shares of other companies and advanced loans to group companies amounting to more than 50% of its total assets. However, trading income constitutes the majority of its total income. Is the company an NBFC?
Q.a:
Rule: a company is an NBFC only if both limbs of the principal-business test are met — financial assets >50% of total assets (net of intangibles) and income from financial assets >50% of gross income.

Analysis: Satyam Pvt Ltd meets the asset-side test (investments + group loans >50% of total assets) but fails the income-side test, since trading income (not financial-asset income) is the majority of total income.

Conclusion: Satyam Pvt Ltd cannot be classified as a (deemed) NBFC — fulfilling only one limb is not enough.
Q.trap: Concluding NBFC status from the asset test alone — ICAI's answer turns entirely on the fact that the income test is not met.

Q.q: Shivam & Co LLP audit an NBFC-Investment and Credit Company (NBFC-ICC). New team members, taking over from those who've left, discuss verification procedures with the departing members. Explain the verification procedures that should be performed for an NBFC-ICC.
Q.a: Verification procedures: physically verify shares/securities held (or obtain a bank/institution custody certificate); confirm no loan is advanced against the NBFC's own shares; verify dividend/interest income is duly received/accounted (dividend on cash basis by default, accrual only once declared at AGM with the right to receive established; bond/debenture interest accrued only if predetermined-rate and regularly serviced); test-check broker contract notes against market quotations; verify Board minutes/certificate support investment acquisition/disposal and current-vs-long-term classification; check valuation and provisioning for market-value falls per Prudential Norms; obtain a subsidiary/group-company investment list and verify pricing basis; verify unquoted debentures/bonds treated as investments (not loans) for income-recognition/classification purposes; verify AS 13 compliance; obtain depository confirmations for dematerialised holdings; confirm securities-lending transactions return the same type/class with corporate benefits; verify single/group borrower concentration limits are respected; check asset classification into Standard/Sub-standard/Doubtful/Loss and provisioning adequacy.
Q.trap: Treating this as a generic investment-audit answer — the ICC-specific points (own-share loan prohibition, dividend cash-basis default, unquoted-debenture reclassification) are what distinguish the model answer.

Q.q: You are appointed auditor of an NBFC registered with RBI that accepts and holds public deposits. What points must you know regarding the separate report to the Board of Directors required in addition to your s.143, Companies Act, 2013 report?
Q.a: Points to know: the additional Board report, under the NBFC Auditor's Report (RBI) Directions, 2016, must cover (for a deposit-accepting NBFC, beyond the matters common to all NBFCs — CoR validity, continued Principal Business Criteria compliance, NOF adequacy): public deposits plus specified other borrowings staying within the permissible ceiling; any excess regularised per the Directions; no acceptance without minimum investment-grade credit rating; CRAR correctly determined and compliant; the rating (per scheme) in force and the deposit ceiling it allows not breached; no violation of acceptance restrictions; no default to depositors on interest/principal; prudential-norms compliance; liquid-assets compliance with the designated-bank communication to RBI; timely filing of the deposit return and the quarterly prudential-norms return; compliance on branch opening/closure/agent appointment.
Q.trap: Reciting only the all-NBFC matters (CoR/NOF) — a deposit-accepting NBFC's report has a substantial extra set of points the question is specifically asking for.

Q.q: Kamna & Co LLP completed the audit of an NBFC; the field team has observations but limited understanding of what exceptions must be reported. Explain the auditor's obligations regarding exceptions in the report.
Q.a:
Obligation: where any matter in the Board report is unfavourable/qualified, or the auditor's opinion is that the NBFC has not complied with Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act, the Public Deposits Directions, or the Scale Based Regulation Directions, 2023, the auditor must send a separate exception report (with full details) to the concerned Regional Office of DNBS having jurisdiction over the company's registered office.

Scope of the duty: it is limited to reporting contraventions only — the exception report must not contain any statement about compliance.
Q.trap: Writing a report that also certifies the matters the NBFC did comply with — the Directions are explicit that only contraventions are to be reported.

Q.q: The statutory auditor of an NBFC must give a report to the Board of Directors. What should its content cover?
Q.a: Content, all NBFCs: whether a valid CoR has been obtained for the non-banking financial activity being conducted; whether, if CoR is held, the company is still entitled to hold it per the Principal Business Criteria as at year-end; whether the NOF requirement under the Scale Based Regulation Directions, 2023 is met. Additionally, for deposit-accepting NBFCs: the deposit-ceiling, rating, CRAR and default-related matters at T28. For non-deposit-accepting NBFCs: Board resolution of non-acceptance passed, no deposits actually accepted, prudential-norms compliance, CRAR (Form NBS-7) correctness and timely filing, and correct MFI classification if applicable.
Q.trap: Not distinguishing the "all NBFCs" baseline from the deposit-accepting vs non-deposit-accepting add-ons — the question structure itself (A/B/C/D in the Directions) is what ICAI's marking scheme follows.

Q.q: Krishna Pvt Ltd meets the Principal Business Criteria at the balance-sheet date (financial assets >50% of total assets, financial income >50% of gross income). What is the obligation of the statutory auditor in such a scenario?
Q.a:
Analysis: meeting both limbs of the Principal Business Criteria means Krishna Pvt Ltd qualifies as an NBFC and is therefore required to hold a Certificate of Registration with RBI.

Obligation: the statutory auditor has an obligation to submit an exception report to RBI on the matters at T29 where the statement on any Board-report item is unfavourable/qualified, or where the company hasn't complied with Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act, the Public Deposits Directions, or the Scale Based Regulation Directions, 2023 — reporting contraventions only, to the relevant Regional Office of DNBS.
Q.trap: Treating "meets the criteria" as the end of the analysis — the real ask is what the auditor does next (the exception-reporting duty), not just the classification conclusion.

Q.q: Mr. G, auditor of LMP Ltd (an NBFC), wants to confirm its FS follow the MCA's 11 October 2018 Division III format (Schedule III, Companies Act, 2013) for Ind-AS NBFCs, and wants to know the presentation differences from Division II. Guide Mr. G.
Q.a:
Differences, Division III (NBFCs) vs Division II: NBFCs may present the balance sheet in order of liquidity (not allowed for Division II companies); NBFCs separately disclose any 'other income'/'other expenditure' item exceeding 1% of total income (Division II: 1% of revenue from operations or ₹10 lakh, whichever is higher); NBFCs separately disclose, under receivables, debts due from any LLP in which a director is a partner/member; NBFCs disclose 'revenue from operations' and 'other comprehensive income' on the face of the P&L, not only in notes; separate disclosure of trade receivables with significant credit-risk increase/credit-impairment; statutory-reserve distribution conditions/restrictions separately disclosed in notes.

Also asked (ICAI): PYQ May 2023 · Q4(b) (re-dated, 'Legal Finance Ltd').
Q.trap: Saying there's "no material difference" between Division II and III — that's the exact wrong conclusion the question is testing (CA R's contention in the PYQ version is marked incorrect for saying this).

Q.q: Abhimanyu Finance Ltd, an NBFC accepting public deposits and giving loans since 2015, had Net Owned Funds of ₹1,50,00,000 and no RBI registration certificate, applying for one only on 30 March 2024. Mr. Kabra was appointed statutory auditor for 2023-24. Advise on the audit procedures and CARO 2020 reporting requirements.
Q.a:
Rule (CARO 2020 cl. 3(xvi)(a)): the auditor reports whether the company is required to register under s.45-IA, RBI Act, 1934, and if so, whether registration has actually been obtained.

Audit procedures: examine the company's RBI-Act-relevant transactions; check the financial statements against the 50%/50% principal-business test; check whether NOF meets the prescribed requirement (here, the prescribed minimum is ₹2 crore, and Abhimanyu's NOF is only ₹1.50 crore — below the requirement); where registration hasn't been obtained, document management's reasons.

Conclusion: Abhimanyu Finance Ltd is a Non-Banking Finance Company carrying on NBFC business since 2015 without ever holding a CoR (application made only on 30 March 2024, with NOF also short of the requirement) — the auditor is required to report this under Clause (xvi) of Paragraph 3, CARO 2020, stating that registration was required but had not been obtained as at the reporting date (an application being pending is not the same as registration having been granted).
Q.trap: Treating the 30 March 2024 application as curing the defect — what CARO 2020 asks is whether registration has been obtained, not merely applied for.

Q.q: Yo-Yo Finance Limited is an NBFC-ML per RBI's revised categorisation. YAK & Associates are Statutory Auditors for 2023-24; the newly-appointed Audit Manager, with limited NBFC-audit exposure, asks the Engagement Partner CA Y what audit procedures verify the company has followed Prudential Norms. As Engagement Partner, suggest any four procedures.
Q.a:
Four procedures: (i) check compliance with prudential norms covering income recognition, income from investments, accounting standards/accounting for investments, asset classification, provisioning for bad/doubtful debts, capital adequacy, the prohibition on loans against the NBFC's own shares, the prohibition on loans/investments where public deposits haven't been repaid, and credit/investment concentration norms; (ii) ensure the Board has framed and implemented a policy for granting/intending to grant demand/call loans; (iii) assess whether advances/credit facilities are properly classified Standard/Sub-standard/Doubtful/Loss with adequate provisioning per the Directions; (iv) check that unrealised NPA income has not been taken to P&L on an accrual basis (realisation basis only), and that an account once classified NPA continues to be shown as such unless genuinely regularised.

Also asked (ICAI): PYQ May 2024 · Q6(c) (identical fact pattern).
Q.trap: Answering with generic "review internal controls" language instead of the four specific, numbered compliance checks ICAI's marking scheme rewards.

Q.q: Singh Ltd, registered under the Companies Act, 2013, is engaged in loans and advances and acquisition of shares/stocks/bonds/debentures/securities issued by government or local authorities. For the year ended 31 March 2024: Paid-up share capital ₹50cr; Non-current assets — loans & advances ₹61.75cr; Current assets — loans & advances ₹312.25cr; Total assets ₹620cr; Intangible assets ₹12cr; Profit for the year ₹7.25cr; Income from interest & dividends ₹68cr; Gross income ₹118.75cr. The directors intend to apply for NBFC registration under s.45-IA, RBI Act, 1934. Advise.
Q.a:
Computation: Financial assets = ₹61.75cr + ₹312.25cr = ₹374 crore. Total assets net of intangibles = ₹620cr − ₹12cr = ₹608 crore → financial assets/total assets = 374/608 = 61.5% (>50%). Income from financial assets = ₹68 crore; Gross income = ₹118.75 crore → 68/118.75 = 57.3% (>50%).

Conclusion: both limbs of the principal-business test are satisfied, so Singh Ltd qualifies as an NBFC and can apply for registration under s.45-IA, RBI Act, 1934, in the prescribed form with the necessary documents.
Q.trap: Forgetting to net off intangible assets from total assets before computing the asset-side percentage.
nums: Financial assets as % of total assets (net of intangibles)
Income from financial assets as % of gross income

Q.q: Suban Engineering, a borrower of the branch, had fully utilised its sanctioned cash credit limit of ₹400 lakh, with an outstanding balance of ₹413 lakh as at 31 March 2024. The bank classified the account as a Sub-standard Asset. On inspection, the DGM found the borrower's premises damaged with no machinery, stock or other assets; the borrower was unreachable, and independent verification confirmed no mortgaged security was available except a piece of land with realisable value ₹33 lakh. The bank accepted this and made a provision treating the account as Sub-standard. Whether correct classification and provisioning norms have been applied?
opts: The account is correctly classified, but provision should be made for 100% of the unsecured portion besides the specified provision on the secured portion.
The account should have been classified as Doubtful, with 100% provision on the unsecured portion besides the required provision on the secured portion.
The account should have been classified as Loss and full provision should have been made in the books of account.
The account should have been classified as Doubtful and full provision should have been made in the books of account.
Q.why: Outstanding ₹413 lakh is covered by realisable security of only ₹33 lakh — virtually total erosion of recoverable value, with the borrower unreachable and no other assets. This is exactly the Loss-asset trigger (non-recoverability due to security-value erosion), not merely Sub-standard or Doubtful — so full (100%) provisioning for a Loss asset is required, not a tiered Doubtful-asset provision.
Q.a: Answer: (c) Loss asset, full provision required — the near-total erosion of security value (₹33 lakh against ₹413 lakh outstanding) and the borrower's unreachability point to a Loss asset, not Sub-standard/Doubtful.

Q.q: DEF Finance Limited is an Investment and Credit Company (ICC) incorporated in March 2020, total assets ₹1,200 crore as at 31 March 2024, meeting the principal-business criteria, currently with Net Owned Funds of ₹8 crore. What is the minimum NOF requirement DEF Finance Limited must achieve by 31 March 2027?
opts: ₹2 crore
₹7 crore
₹10 crore
₹8 crore
Q.why: NBFC-ICCs are on a glide path to the general minimum NOF of ₹10 crore by 31 March 2027 (₹5cr by 31.3.2025, ₹10cr by 31.3.2027) — ₹8 crore already held is not yet the final target, and ₹2cr/₹7cr are earlier glide-path milestones, not the 2027 figure.
Q.a: Answer: (c) ₹10 crore by 31 March 2027, per the NBFC-ICC NOF glide path.

Q.q: SH Finance Limited, an NBFC registered with RBI under the Middle Layer category, classified a demand loan of ₹3.8 crore to RR Traders as NPA on 1 September 2023. Estimated realisable security value is ₹2.2 crore; the company has made a provision of ₹1.6 crore (100% of the unsecured portion). For F.Y. 2024-25 (year ended 31 March 2025), what is the correct asset classification and minimum total provisioning required?
opts: Sub-standard Asset with provision of ₹1.98 crore
Doubtful Asset with provision of ₹2.26 crore
Doubtful Asset with provision of ₹2.04 crore
Loss Asset with provision of ₹3.8 crore
Q.why: For NBFC-ML and above, an account stays Sub-standard for only 12 months as NPA; beyond that it is Doubtful. NPA since 1.9.2023 means by 31.3.2025 it has been NPA ~19 months — past the 12-month cut, so Doubtful. Provision = 100% of unsecured portion (₹3.8cr − ₹2.2cr = ₹1.6cr) + 20% of the secured ₹2.2cr (doubtful for under a year, since the Doubtful clock itself only started ~Sept 2024) = ₹1.6cr + ₹0.44cr = ₹2.04cr.
Q.a: Answer: (c) Doubtful Asset, provision ₹2.04 crore (₹1.6cr unsecured @100% + ₹0.44cr secured @20%, under the Middle Layer's 12-month sub-standard cut).

Q.q: SH Finance Limited has invested ₹45 crore in approved liquid assets and held them in safe custody at its own premises. What should CA L's observation be regarding this custody arrangement?
opts: The arrangement is acceptable as approved liquid assets can be held in the company's own custody.

The company should lodge these liquid assets in safe custody with a designated scheduled commercial bank as required by the NBFC Acceptance of Public Deposits Directions, and also obtain a certificate from RBI to that effect.
Safe custody arrangement is not relevant for audit purposes.
Approved liquid assets need not be lodged with banks as they are risk-free assets.
Q.why: The Public Deposits Directions require approved liquid assets to be lodged in safe custody with a designated scheduled commercial bank, with an RBI certificate confirming this — an NBFC cannot simply hold them on its own premises, however 'safe' it considers that to be.
Q.a: Answer: (b) — must be lodged with a designated scheduled commercial bank, with an RBI certificate to that effect.

Q.q: At Kochi Branch of KLM Bank Limited, the auditor identifies: (i) QT Ltd's term loan ₹5cr sanctioned at 9.5% p.a. but the CBS reflects 8.5% p.a. w.e.f. 1.4.2024; (ii) NK Pvt Ltd's working-capital limit ₹3cr carries a mandated 1% processing fee, but only 0.5% was charged; (iii) DEF Ltd's CC limit ₹4cr required monthly stock statements — not submitted for 3 months, triggering 2% p.a. penal interest; (iv) GHI Exports' packing credit ₹2cr at 6% p.a. for 3 months was repaid 1 month late, attracting 12% p.a. overdue interest not applied in the CBS. Calculate the revenue leakage for the year.
Q.why: (i) (9.5%−8.5%)×₹5cr = ₹5,00,000. (ii) 1%×₹3cr − 0.5%×₹3cr = ₹1,50,000. (iii) 2%×₹4cr×3/12 = ₹2,00,000. (iv) overdue interest on the 1-month delay: ICAI accepted both the full 12% p.a. (₹2,00,000, giving ₹10,50,000 total) and the incremental 12%−6%=6% p.a. over the normal rate (₹1,00,000, giving ₹9,50,000 total) as correct — this option is one of ICAI's two accepted answers.
Q.a: Answer: (a) or (d) — ICAI accepted both ₹9,50,000 (incremental overdue rate) and ₹10,50,000 (full overdue rate on item iv); items (i)–(iii) total ₹8,50,000 either way.

Q.q: Easy Finance Limited (NBFC) reports, as at 31 March 2025: Cash and bank balances incl. FDs/CDs with banks ₹8cr; Investments — bonds of public financial institutions ₹50cr; Current assets — loans to staff ₹5cr; Fixed assets (net) — furniture & fixtures ₹30cr; Domestic Sovereign — State-Government-guaranteed claims in default for 75 days ₹60cr. Calculate the aggregate risk-adjusted value of these funded assets for reckoning the minimum capital ratio.
opts: ₹110 crore
₹92 crore
₹115 crore
₹52 crore
Q.why: Risk weights: cash/bank balances 0% (₹8cr → 0); PFI bonds 100% (₹50cr → ₹50cr); loans to staff 0% (₹5cr → 0); furniture & fixtures 100% (₹30cr → ₹30cr); State-Govt-guaranteed claims in default ≤90 days 20% (₹60cr → ₹12cr). Total = 50+30+12 = ₹92 crore.
Q.a: Answer: (b) ₹92 crore = ₹50cr (bonds@100%) + ₹30cr (fixed assets@100%) + ₹12cr (State-Govt-guaranteed, in default ≤90 days@20%); cash/bank and staff loans carry 0% weight.

Q.q: At the Indore Main branch, the audit team splits advances work: Mr. X focuses on evaluating internal control over advances, Mr. Y on substantive audit procedures, Mr. Z on recoverability of advances. From the following procedures — (i) examine security existence/enforceability/valuation; (ii) verify correctness of CBS master data (instalments, EMI, rate, tenure); (iii) examine whether the system for review/renewal of advances is followed; (iv) examine problem accounts not yet NPA via SMA-1/SMA-2 lists; (v) review auditor's reports of borrowers with credit facilities beyond a board cut-off — which should Mr. Y (substantive procedures) focus upon?
opts: (i), (ii), (iii)
(ii) and (iv)
(iii) and (iv)
Q.why: (ii) CBS master-data verification and (iv) SMA-1/SMA-2 problem-account examination are substantive procedures testing actual transaction/balance correctness. (i) security existence/enforceability is an internal-control evaluation point (Mr. X's area); (iii) review/renewal-system compliance is also a control-evaluation point; (v) borrower auditor's-report review is a recoverability check (Mr. Z's area).
Q.a: Answer: (c) (ii) and (iv) — CBS master-data checks and SMA-1/2 examination are the substantive-procedure items; the rest split across internal-control evaluation and recoverability.

Q.q: Kiran Ltd, a trading company, has a cash credit facility of ₹10 crore (sanctioned limit ₹1,000 lakh) from Indore Main branch. At 31 March 2025: Total stock ₹900 lakh (incl. ₹60 lakh damaged); Total receivables ₹800 lakh (ageing: 0–30 days ₹250L, 31–60 ₹200L, 61–90 ₹250L, >90 days ₹100L); Creditors for stock ₹140 lakh; Margin on stock 25%; Margin on receivables 40%. What is the Drawing Power (DP) available to Kiran Ltd?
opts: ₹1,005 lakh
₹1,000 lakh
₹945 lakh
₹990 lakh
Q.why: Eligible stock = (900 − 60 damaged − 140 creditors for stock) × (1 − 25%) = 700 × 75% = ₹525 lakh. Eligible receivables exclude the >90-day overdue bucket: (800 − 100) × (1 − 40%) = 700 × 60% = ₹420 lakh. DP = 525 + 420 = ₹945 lakh (within the ₹1,000 lakh sanctioned limit).

Q.q: APP Ltd, an NBFC that got itself registered with RBI fulfilling the required criteria, accepted deposits of ₹900 crore during FY 2024-25 while its asset size is ₹990 crore. It has also undertaken activities as a Standalone Primary Dealer (SPD), Infrastructure Debt Fund (IDF), Housing Finance and Infrastructure Finance. Under which layer will APP Ltd be categorised?
opts: Top Layer
Upper Layer
Middle Layer
Base Layer
Q.why: APP Ltd is a deposit-taking NBFC (accepted ₹900cr in deposits) — all deposit-taking NBFCs (NBFC-D) sit in the Middle Layer irrespective of asset size. Its SPD/IDF/HFC/IFC activities independently also always place it in the Middle Layer, reinforcing the same answer; ₹990cr asset size (just under ₹1,000cr) is a red herring since activity/deposit-taking status decides this, not the size test.
Q.a: Answer: (c) Middle Layer — deposit-taking status alone fixes this regardless of size; the SPD/IDF/HFC/IFC activities confirm the same layer.

Q.q: Maha Bank Limited's DTL balance as on 30 September 2024 was ₹50,000 crore, which included: Paid-up capital ₹27,000cr; Reserves ₹1,650cr; Credit balance in P&L ₹1,210cr; Loan taken from RBI ₹575cr; Refinance from EXIM Bank and NHB ₹480cr; Part recoveries from borrowers on debts considered bad/doubtful ₹125cr; Net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts ₹105cr; Interest accrued but not accounted for in books ₹90cr; Margins held in sundry deposits for funded facilities ₹80cr. Compute the correct DTL balance as on 30 September 2024.
opts: ₹18,000 crore
₹19,360 crore
₹18,790 crore
₹18,880 crore
Q.why: Exclude from the reported ₹50,000cr: paid-up capital (27,000) + reserves (1,650) + P&L credit balance (1,210) + RBI loan (575) + EXIM/NHB refinance (480) + bad-debt recoveries (125) + sundry-deposit margins (80) = ₹31,120cr. The branch-adjustment credit balance (₹105cr) and interest accrued-but-unbooked (₹90cr) are items the RBI rules require to be *included* in DTL — since the question states they are already part of the ₹50,000cr reported figure, no further adjustment is needed for them. Corrected DTL = 50,000 − 31,120 = ₹18,880 crore.
Q.a: Answer: (d) ₹18,880 crore = ₹50,000cr less the seven items RBI excludes from DTL (capital, reserves, P&L credit, RBI loan, EXIM/NHB refinance, bad-debt recoveries, sundry-deposit margins = ₹31,120cr); the branch-adjustment credit balance and unbooked interest accrued stay in, as RBI requires.

Q.q: Which statute gives the Reserve Bank of India wide powers to issue directions to all banks (not only banking companies as defined)?
opts: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The Companies Act, 2013
The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007
Q.why: The BR Act, 1949 is the core banking-business statute, but the RBI Act, 1934 is the source of RBI's general directions power over banks. The Companies Act and PSS Act govern narrower areas (corporate law; payment systems).
Q.a: Answer: (b) The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.

Q.q: A firm currently holds an internal-assignment engagement with a bank. Per RBI's rule on internal assignments, can the same firm also take up the bank's statutory audit for the same year?
opts: Yes, there is no restriction
No — RBI has decided audit firms should not hold the statutory audit while associated with internal assignments in the same bank in the same year
Yes, provided the Board approves
Only if the internal assignment is unrelated to financial reporting
Q.why: This is a flat RBI-decided bar for the same year, not something a Board approval can waive, and not conditioned on the nature of the internal assignment.
Q.a: Answer: (b) — the bar applies regardless of Board approval or the nature of the internal assignment.

Q.q: A bank outsources its data-entry processing to a third-party vendor to cut costs. Who remains responsible for managing the risks this outsourcing creates?
opts: The vendor, since the activity itself is delegated
The bank — outsourcing an activity doesn't outsource the responsibility to manage its risk
RBI, since it approved the outsourcing policy
No one — outsourced risk falls outside the audit scope
Q.why: Outsourcing shifts who performs the activity, not who bears responsibility for the risk it creates — the SM is explicit that the bank must still effectively manage outsourcing risk, and the auditor must specifically evaluate this.
Q.a: Answer: (b) The bank remains responsible for managing outsourcing risk.

Q.q: Under Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA), how is a branch's priority for audit coverage decided?
opts: Alphabetically by branch name
By a risk matrix combining inherent business risk and the effectiveness of controls mitigating it
By branch age alone
Every branch gets identical coverage each year
Q.why: RBIA identifies inherent business risks by activity, assesses control effectiveness over those risks, and draws a risk matrix per branch to decide direction/level of overall risk — that matrix, not alphabetical order or age, drives audit priority.
Q.a: Answer: (b) A risk matrix combining business risk and control risk.

Q.q: Which of these is an internal-control failure in a bank's cash-handling area?
opts: Cash kept in joint custody of two officers
The cashier also has access to the customer ledger and day book
High-value cash receipts verified by a senior officer
Daily independent arithmetical checking of cash
Q.why: The SM is explicit that the cashier must have NO access to the customer ledger/day book — allowing it can let a cashier manipulate both cash and records undetected. The other three options are the correct controls, not failures.
Q.a: Answer: (b) — cashier access to the ledger/day book is the one listed item that is a control failure, not a safeguard.

Q.q: Under RBI guidelines, for an inward-clearing cheque of what amount and above must the branch call or email the customer before honouring it?
opts: ₹1 lakh and above
₹2 lakh and above
₹5 lakh and above
₹10 lakh and above
Q.why: The SM states the ₹5 lakh threshold specifically for inward clearing under CTS — the auditor verifies this on a test-check basis.
Q.a: Answer: (c) ₹5 lakh and above.

Q.q: Two bank branches each hold call-loan balances — one lent ₹20 lakh at call, the other borrowed ₹15 lakh at call from a different bank. Can these be netted in the balance sheet?
opts: Yes, always net call loans against call borrowings
No — call loans made by a bank cannot be netted against call loans received
Only if both are with the same counterparty bank
Netting is permitted only at year-end
Q.why: The SM is explicit on this point for 'Money at Call and Short Notice' verification: lending and borrowing positions in call money are shown gross, not netted, regardless of counterparty.
Q.a: Answer: (b) — call loans made cannot be netted against call loans received.

Q.q: A bank's investment is overdue on both interest and principal, unpaid for 95 days. How should it be classified and treated for income purposes?
opts: Still a performing investment since 95 days is under the NPA threshold for advances
A Non-Performing Investment (NPI) — income is not recognised and depreciation provision is required
Automatically shifted from AFS to HTM
Written off entirely regardless of recoverable value
Q.why: An investment unpaid for more than 90 days is an NPI — distinct from the advances NPA concept but with a parallel effect: no income recognition, and a depreciation provision is required.
Q.a: Answer: (b) NPI treatment — no income recognition, provision for depreciation in value.

Q.q: For how long can a banking company hold immovable property acquired in satisfaction of a debt, before Section 9 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 requires it to dispose of (or justify retaining) it for the bank's own use?
opts: 3 years
5 years
7 years
10 years
Q.why: Section 9, BR Act, 1949 bars holding immovable property for more than 7 years from acquisition, except property required for the bank's own use.
Q.a: Answer: (c) 7 years.

Q.q: At what value should a non-banking asset (NBA) acquired by a bank in satisfaction of a claim be recorded on acquisition?
opts: Fair market value of the asset
Lower of the net book value of the advance or the net realisable value of the asset acquired
Higher of the two values, to be conservative in reverse
Original cost to the defaulting borrower
Q.why: The SM specifically prescribes recording at the lower of net book value of the advance or net realisable value of the acquired asset — a conservative rule to avoid overstating the asset.
Q.a: Answer: (b) Lower of NBV of the advance or NRV of the asset.

Q.q: Even where a bank's advance is classified as a Standard Asset, is any provision still required against it?
opts: No, Standard assets never require provisioning
Yes — a prudential provision is required at variable rates by sector for funded outstandings, as a matter of prudence
Yes, but only for advances above ₹1 crore
Only for foreign-currency-denominated standard advances
Q.why: The SM is explicit that Standard-asset provisioning is still required, at rates that vary by sector, purely as a matter of prudence — it isn't size- or currency-conditioned.
Q.a: Answer: (b) — sector-variable provisioning is required even for Standard assets.

Q.q: A bank wants to utilise its Share Premium Account for a purpose not permitted by the governing legislation. What should the auditor specifically check?
opts: Nothing — share premium utilisation is entirely a management decision
That the appropriation from Share Premium conforms to the relevant legal requirements
Only the Board resolution authorising the transfer
Whether shareholders were informed after the fact
Q.why: The SM requires the auditor to specifically examine whether appropriations from the share premium account conform to the relevant legal requirements — this is a compliance check, not simply a governance/disclosure matter.
Q.a: Answer: (b) Check conformity of the appropriation with the governing legal requirements.

Q.q: Which deposit account type is repatriable, and which is not (except for current income, subject to conditions)?
opts: NRE repatriable; NRO not repatriable
NRO repatriable; NRE not repatriable
Both are fully repatriable
Neither is repatriable
Q.why: NRE accounts (opened by NRIs/PIOs) are repatriable; NRO accounts (open to any non-resident) are not repatriable except current income subject to conditions — a frequently-confused pair.
Q.a: Answer: (a) NRE repatriable, NRO not (except current income).

Q.q: A bank rediscounts a bill with another bank. Under which Schedule III head does this appear?
opts: 'Borrowings' — rediscounting is treated identically to refinance
It does not figure under 'Borrowings' — rediscount and refinance must be clearly distinguished
'Other Liabilities and Provisions'
'Contingent Liabilities'
Q.why: The SM draws a specific line: rediscount does not figure under the Borrowings head, while refinance does — the auditor must examine whether this distinction has been correctly made in disclosure.
Q.a: Answer: (b) — rediscount is excluded from Borrowings; only refinance belongs there.

Q.q: In the balance sheet, are a bank's Advances and Investments figures shown gross or net of the provisions held against them?
opts: Gross, with provisions shown only in notes
Net — already reduced by provisions held to the auditor's satisfaction
Gross for Advances, net for Investments
It varies bank to bank with no fixed rule
Q.why: The SM specifically notes that the advances and investments figures exclude provisions made against them to the auditor's satisfaction — i.e. they're shown net, not gross with a note.
Q.a: Answer: (b) Net of provisions, to the auditor's satisfaction.

Q.q: Does the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 (CARO) apply to the statutory audit of a banking company?
opts: Yes, in full
Yes, but only the clauses relating to loans and investments
No — CARO 2020 does not apply to a banking company as defined in s.5(c), BR Act, 1949
Only for private-sector banks, not public-sector banks
Q.why: The SM is explicit: CARO 2020 reporting requirements do not apply to a banking company as defined under the BR Act — a frequently tested negative point, in contrast to NBFCs, where specific CARO clauses (3(iii), 3(xvi)) do apply.
Q.a: Answer: (c) CARO 2020 does not apply to banking companies at all.

Q.q: Within how many days of the SCA's submission of the bank-level LFAR must a copy (with the ACB's views/directions) be sent to RBI?
opts: 30 days
45 days
60 days
90 days
Q.why: The SM specifies 60 days from the auditor's LFAR submission for the ACB-reviewed copy (with agenda note and Board's views) to reach RBI.
Q.a: Answer: (c) 60 days.

Q.q: Does an auditor need to examine every single transaction to meet the fraud-reporting responsibility under s.143(12), Companies Act, 2013?
opts: Yes, every transaction must be individually examined
No — the auditor evaluates the system as a whole, not every transaction
Only transactions above ₹1 crore need examination
Only cash transactions need examination
Q.why: The SM explicitly states the auditor is not expected to consider every transaction, only to evaluate the system as a whole — if a fraud instance comes to notice in the ordinary course, it's reported to RBI and the bank's Chairman/MD/CEO.
Q.a: Answer: (b) — system-level evaluation, not transaction-by-transaction examination.

Q.q: What is the maximum continuous tenure an external concurrent auditor firm may have (i) with the bank overall, and (ii) with any one branch/business unit?
opts: 3 years overall; 5 years per branch
5 years overall; 3 years per branch
5 years overall; 5 years per branch
No tenure limit applies to concurrent auditors
Q.why: The SM fixes 5 years as the general bank-wide continuous-tenure ceiling, but only 3 years with any single branch/business unit — the two limits often get swapped by students.
Q.a: Answer: (b) 5 years with the bank overall; 3 years with any one branch.

Q.q: Which of these is NOT a function of a bank's Audit Committee of the Board (ACB)?
opts: Directing and overseeing the bank's total audit function
Reviewing internal inspection/audit system quality and follow-up effectiveness
Reviewing appointment, remuneration and quality of concurrent auditors
Signing the bank's statutory audit report on behalf of the SCAs
Q.why: The ACB directs/oversees and reviews the audit function (internal and concurrent audit) — but it does not itself sign the statutory audit report, which remains the SCAs' own responsibility.
Q.a: Answer: (d) — signing the statutory report is the SCAs' job, not the ACB's.

Q.q: Which of the following is available to a bank depositor but NOT to an NBFC depositor?
opts: Term deposit facility
DICGC deposit insurance cover
Ability to earn interest
A passbook or statement
Q.why: DICGC deposit insurance specifically covers bank deposits, not NBFC deposits — one of the four textbook NBFC-vs-bank differences.
Q.a: Answer: (b) DICGC cover is not available to NBFC depositors.

Q.q: An NBFC's advance became non-performing in June. It had recognised ₹2 lakh of interest income on this advance on an accrual basis in April and May, before it turned NPA, which remains unrealised. What should happen to this ₹2 lakh?
opts: It stays recognised — income already booked before an asset turns NPA is never reversed
It must be reversed, since it remains unrealised
Only half needs to be reversed
It converts automatically into a provision, not a reversal
Q.why: The SM's NBFC income-recognition rule: income recognised before the asset became non-performing and remaining unrealised must be reversed — the earlier accrual basis doesn't protect it once the asset turns NPA.
Q.a: Answer: (b) Reverse the unrealised ₹2 lakh.

Q.q: A cash shortage of ₹6,000 is first detected by the branch's internal inspector (not self-reported by the cashier on occurrence). Must this be reported as fraud even though no intent to cheat is proved?
opts: No — cash shortages are reported as fraud only if intent is proved, regardless of amount
Yes — shortages above ₹5,000, if first detected by management/auditor/inspecting officer rather than self-reported, are treated as fraud regardless of proven intent
Only shortages above ₹10,000 ever require reporting
Reporting is optional, left to branch manager discretion
Q.why: The two-tier exception: shortages >₹10,000 are reported as fraud regardless of how detected; shortages >₹5,000 are reported as fraud specifically when caught by management/auditor/inspector rather than self-reported by the handler on occurrence — ₹6,000, inspector-detected, fits the second limb.
Q.a: Answer: (b) — the ₹5,000 threshold applies here since detection was by the inspector, not self-reported.

Q.q: Which rule brings NBFCs within the ambit of Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)?
opts: Rule 4(1)(iv), Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015
Section 133, Companies Act, 2013, standalone
RBI Master Direction on NBFC Returns
SEBI LODR Regulations
Q.why: Rule 4(1)(iv) of the Companies (Ind AS) Rules, 2015 (as amended by the 2023 Amendment Rules) is the specific provision bringing NBFCs under Ind AS — s.133 is the enabling Companies Act section but the applicability mechanics sit in the Rules.
Q.a: Answer: (a) Rule 4(1)(iv), Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015.

Q.q: During the statutory audit of Fair Bank, you examine the Cash Credit account of M/s Bright Traders as at 31 March 2025: Sanctioned limit ₹4 crore; Outstanding ₹4.10 crore; Excess over limit ₹10 lakh for 15 days; Latest stock statement dated 31 January 2025; Renewal of limit was due 28 February 2025 and is under process; Interest is regularly serviced, no amount overdue beyond 90 days; Drawing Power is properly calculated based on a stock statement less than 3 months old. The Branch Manager has treated the account as a Standard Asset. Examine whether the account requires classification as NPA.
Q.a:
Rule: banks should not classify an advance as NPA merely because of temporary deficiencies — non-availability of drawing power based on the latest stock statement, the balance temporarily exceeding the limit, or non-renewal of limits by the due date — provided the stock statement relied on for drawing power is not older than 3 months (an outstanding based on a stale statement older than 3 months is irregular).

Analysis: the ₹10 lakh excess has lasted only 15 days; the stock statement (31 Jan 2025) is within 3 months of the balance-sheet date; the renewal, though due, is genuinely under process; interest is being serviced regularly and nothing is overdue beyond 90 days.

Conclusion: since every deficiency here is purely temporary, drawing power rests on a statement under 3 months old, and the account hasn't been out of order for more than 90 days, the account should not be classified as NPA — the Branch Manager's treatment as a Standard Asset is correct per RBI IRAC norms.
Q.trap: Flagging the account as NPA on the strength of the limit excess or the pending renewal alone — both are exactly the kind of temporary deficiency the rule is written to exclude, provided the 3-month stock-statement and 90-day conditions hold.

Q.q: Nutan & Co, statutory auditor of JOE Bank Ltd (a private sector bank), noted the following audit queries: (1) an NPA was sold for a value higher than net book value — profit was not recognised, but the excess provision was reversed; (2) interest on a State-Government-guaranteed advance has been taken to income even though the advance is overdue for more than 90 days; (3) an account's ad hoc limit has not been reviewed for 180 days from the ad hoc sanction date, and the account is treated as performing; (4) on verifying outstanding forward exchange contracts, the 'net position' for one foreign currency was not squared and was uncovered by a substantial amount; (5) one account was sanctioned an additional temporary limit of 25% of the existing limit for 120 days. Give the reason for each query and the action that should be taken.
Q.a:
#Reason for the queryAction required
1Where an NPA is sold above net book value, the excess must not be recognised as profit, and the excess provision must not be reversed — it is retained to meet shortfall/loss on sale of other NPAs.Cancel the reversal entry; retain the excess provision to meet shortfall/loss on sale of other non-performing financial assets.
2A State-Government-guaranteed advance must be treated as NPA once overdue beyond 90 days — the Central-Government invoke-and-repudiate carve-out does not extend to State guarantees.Reverse the interest income already recognised; take it to income only when actually realised.
3Accounts where the ad hoc limit isn't reviewed within 180 days of sanction must be treated as NPA.Change the treatment from performing to non-performing asset, from the date the change was required.
4The net position in each foreign currency should generally be squared, not left substantially uncovered.Square off the branch's net position in that currency, covering it by a substantial amount.
5Additional temporary limits may be sanctioned only up to 20% of the existing limit and for a maximum 90-day tenure.Revise the terms of the additional temporary limit to 20% of the existing limit and 90 days' maximum tenure.
Q.trap: Item 1 is the recurring trap across this whole chapter: profit on an above-NBV NPA sale is never booked, and the related excess provision is never reversed.

Q.q: Auditing the branch operations of XS Bank for the year ending 31 March 2025, you observe: advances sanctioned without proper credit appraisal in some cases; loans sanctioned without adequate documentation (DPNs, hypothecation letters) and weak post-disbursement monitoring in others; securities held by a single officer instead of joint custody at several branches; and a few accounts that exceeded sanctioned limit/drawing power without intimation to Head Office. The branch manager says the bank relies on its internal control framework to mitigate such risks. Explain the internal controls the bank is expected to implement in the area of loans and advances.
Q.a:
Expected internal controls over loans and advances: advances only after satisfying creditworthiness and obtaining proper sanction from the bank's authorities; all necessary documents (agreements, DPNs, hypothecation letters etc.) executed before disbursal; sufficient margin kept against securities, determined by proper authority, to cover any decline in value and comply with RBI directives; securities received/returned by a responsible officer and held in joint custody of two officers; registrable securities registered in the bank's name (or adequately documented otherwise); accounts kept within both the drawing power and the sanctioned limit — additional temporary limits capped at 20% of the existing limit and 90 days' tenure; accounts exceeding the sanctioned limit, drawing power, or against unapproved securities, or otherwise irregular, reported to Management/HO regularly; each advance account's operation reviewed at least once a year.

Conclusion: the four observed lapses map directly onto these controls — credit appraisal, pre-disbursal documentation, joint custody of securities, and prompt reporting of limit/DP breaches — and each is an internal-control deficiency, not something an unspecified 'framework' excuses.
Q.trap: Accepting the branch manager's generic reassurance as sufficient — each specific lapse observed corresponds to a named, specific control that was not actually operating.

Q.q: ABC Ltd, a company registered under the Companies Act, 2013, is engaged in the business of loans and advances and acquisition of shares/stocks/bonds/debentures/securities issued by Government or local authorities. For the year ended 31 March 2021: Paid-up share capital ₹40.53cr; Non-current assets — loans & advances ₹55.90cr; Current assets — loans & advances ₹344.47cr; Total assets ₹530cr; Intangible assets ₹3cr; Profit for the year ₹7.25cr; Income from interest & dividends ₹52cr; Gross income ₹102.57cr. Directors intend to apply for registration as an NBFC under s.45-IA, RBI Act, 1934. Advise.
Q.a:
Computation: Financial assets = ₹55.90cr + ₹344.47cr = ₹400.37 crore. Total assets net of intangibles = ₹530cr − ₹3cr = ₹527 crore → 400.37/527 = 76.0% (>50%). Income from financial assets = ₹52 crore; Gross income = ₹102.57 crore → 52/102.57 = 50.7% (>50%).

Conclusion: both limbs of the principal-business test are met, so ABC Ltd qualifies as an NBFC and can apply for registration under s.45-IA, RBI Act, 1934 (Amendment) Act, 1997, with the prescribed documents.

Variant of SM TYK Q12 (Singh Ltd) — same test, different figures.
Q.trap: Forgetting to net off intangible assets (₹3cr) before computing the asset-side percentage.
nums: Financial assets as % of total assets (net of intangibles)
Income from financial assets as % of gross income

Q.q: M/s TZ and Associates, statutory branch auditors of the Delhi Branch of ABC Bank Limited for F.Y. 2024-25, are verifying advances. CA T selects Mr. X's account: a ₹1 crore housing loan from 2021-22, operating positively till 2023-24, often overdue since April 2024. On 1.10.2024 Mr. X requested (due to a medical emergency) an increased repayment period and reduced interest rate; the Branch accepted this on 1.11.2024. The Branch classified the account as a Standard Asset as at 31.3.2025. CA T insists it should be Sub-standard, since there is a change in the terms of payment, and drafts a Memorandum of Changes (MOC). The Board-prescribed rate of provision for the secured portion of a Sub-standard Asset is 20%, while the IRAC-norms requirement is 15%. (i) Justify CA T's classification. (ii) Guide CA T on the rate to apply for the secured portion in the MOC.
Q.a:
(i) Classification: restructuring (modifying terms of advances — here, repayment period and interest rate — for a borrower's financial difficulty) downgrades a Standard account to Sub-standard under RBI prudential norms (an already-NPA account instead stays in its existing NPA category). Mr. X's account was restructured on 1.11.2024 due to financial difficulty, so CA T's insistence on classifying it Sub-standard as at 31.3.2025 is correct — the Branch's Standard-Asset treatment is wrong.

(ii) Provisioning rate: RBI's prescribed provisioning norms are minimum requirements — a bank may always apply a higher rate where warranted. Since IRAC's 15% is a floor, and ABC Bank Ltd's Board has prescribed a higher 20% for the secured portion, the higher 20% rate should be applied in the MOC.
Q.trap: Applying the IRAC minimum (15%) simply because it's the regulatory figure — RBI norms are explicitly a floor, and a bank-prescribed higher rate always governs.

Q.q: Instant Finance Ltd, an NBFC-BL primarily lending to small businesses and individuals, reports for the year ending 31 March 2025: aggregate risk-weighted asset base ₹1,000 crore; reported Tier 1 capital ₹130 crore, which includes ₹15 crore raised through perpetual debt instruments; investments in shares/bonds of other NBFCs totalling ₹10 crore (12% of its owned fund); primary business is lending against gold jewellery, comprising 60% of its financial assets. As statutory auditor assessing compliance with the RBI (Scale Based Regulation) Directions, 2023: (i) evaluate whether minimum Tier I capital requirements are met; (ii) discuss the treatment of perpetual debt instruments in Tier I for gold-loan NBFCs; (iii) analyse the Tier 1 adjustment needed for its investments in other NBFCs.
Q.a:
(i) Minimum requirement: since gold loans are 60% of financial assets (≥50%), Instant Finance Ltd must maintain Tier 1 capital of at least 12% of aggregate risk-weighted assets = 12% × ₹1,000cr = ₹120 crore.

(ii) Perpetual debt treatment: NBFC-BL are not eligible to include perpetual debt instruments in Tier I capital at all — so the reported ₹130cr, which includes ₹15cr of perpetual debt, must be reduced: ₹130cr − ₹15cr = ₹115 crore Tier 1.

(iii) Inter-NBFC investment adjustment (alternative working): Tier I (for non-BL NBFCs) is owned fund reduced by investments in other NBFCs exceeding 10% of owned fund. Here owned fund = ₹10cr ÷ 12% = ₹83.33cr, so the 10% threshold = ₹8.33cr, and the excess over that threshold = ₹10cr − ₹8.33cr = ₹1.667 crore to additionally deduct: ₹130cr − ₹15cr (perpetual debt) − ₹1.667cr = ₹113.33 crore.

Conclusion: whichever working is used (₹115cr or ₹113.33cr), Tier 1 capital is below the required ₹120 crore — Instant Finance Ltd has not complied with the minimum Tier 1 capital requirement.
Q.trap: Using the general 10% Tier I floor instead of the 12% gold-loan-NBFC floor — the 60%-of-financial-assets fact is exactly what triggers the higher requirement.

Q.src: Law changed · RTP May 2026 academic update
Q.q: Gold Trust NBFC primarily lends against gold jewellery (62% of its financial assets) and is an NBFC-ML. Its auditor, reviewing the latest RBI circulars for the Nov 2026 attempt, must confirm: (a) what additional compliance Gold Trust NBFC's Tier 1 capital definition now explicitly requires, and by when; (b) under what circumstance an NBFC-MFI must approach RBI with a remediation plan; (c) what new item has been added to the 'Others (to be specified)' row of the risk-weighted-assets table.
Q.a:
(a) Gold-loan NBFC Tier 1: Gold Trust NBFC's 12% Tier 1 floor (financial assets ≥50% in gold loans) must now be read with the RBI (Lending Against Gold and Silver Collateral) Directions, 2025 (dated 6 June 2025) for on-/off-balance-sheet treatment; compliance was required as expeditiously as possible but not later than 1 April 2026 — a date that has already passed, so full compliance is now assumed, not merely in progress.

(b) NBFC-MFI remediation: an NBFC-MFI must keep at least 60% of total assets (net of intangibles) deployed in microfinance loans on an ongoing basis. If it fails this test for 4 consecutive quarters, it must approach RBI with a remediation plan (circular DoR.FIN.REC.25/03.10.038/2025-26, dated 6 June 2025).

(c) Risk-weight table addition: the 'Others (to be specified)' line under on-balance-sheet weighted risk assets now explicitly includes Right-of-Use (ROU) assets.
Q.trap: Describing the gold-loan Tier 1 compliance deadline as still pending — for the Nov 2026 attempt, 1 April 2026 has already passed, so it's the settled position, not an upcoming one.

Q.q: Varma & Associates is one of four firms jointly appointed as Statutory Central Auditors of a nationalised bank. The engagement partner wants to understand (a) what form the bank's financial statements must take and whether a branch audit is mandatory, and (b) what the SCA appointment letter should cover and who finally approves the appointment. Advise.
Q.a:
(a) Form of FS: the bank must prepare its Balance Sheet and P&L in the forms set out in the Third Schedule to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 — Form A (Balance Sheet) and Form B (P&L) — complying with the applicable Accounting Standards (Ind AS implementation remains deferred by RBI for scheduled commercial banks). Preparing the bank's standalone FS usually means consolidating branch accounts and departments/verticals; separately, consolidated FS are also prepared. Mandatory branch audit applies to nationalised/public-sector banks (hence the joint-SCA structure here) — private banks centralise accounting and have no concept of mandatory branch audit under RBI guidelines.

(b) Appointment letter & approval: the SCA appointment letter typically covers the period of appointment; particulars of the other joint central auditors and of previous auditors; procedural requirements for accepting the assignment (letter of acceptance, declaration of fidelity/secrecy, restriction on accepting other bank assignments); division of work and review/reporting responsibilities among joint auditors (usually fixed at a later stage); and the scope of assignment including any special reports/certificates beyond the main report. For a nationalised bank, the Board of Directors appoints the auditor (not a shareholders' AGM, since there are none in the usual sense) — but in either case (banking company or nationalised bank), RBI's approval is required before the appointment is made.
Q.trap: Assuming every bank needs branch audits — the mandatory-branch-audit concept is specifically a public-sector/nationalised-bank feature, not a universal rule.

Q.q: A newly-formed engagement team for a bank audit is unsure how to sequence its work and what IT-specific information to request at the outset. Set out (a) the five stages of a bank audit in order, and (b) the categories of IT information the bank should share with the auditor given the CBS environment.
Q.a:
(a) Five stages: I. Initial considerations (acceptance & continuance, declaration of indebtedness, bar on internal assignments, SA 210 terms, communication with the previous auditor, planning, forming the engagement team) → II. Understanding (the bank, its environment and internal control; its accounting process; its risk management process) → III. Risk assessment (SA 315 risk of material misstatement; SA 240 fraud/money-laundering risk; specific industry/IT risks; outsourcing risk) → IV. Execution (engagement team discussions; SA 330 responses to assessed risk; SA 300 overall audit strategy; the Audit Planning Memorandum; materiality; going concern) → V. Reporting (the statutory report and LFAR).
