(b) IT information to request: overall IT policy, structure and environment; data-processing and data-interface arrangements across systems; data integrity and security; business-continuity and disaster-recovery plans; the accounting manual and critical accounting entries (and IT involvement in them); controls over key account-head usage and expense booking; controls over e-banking/internet-banking channels; MIS reports and their periodicity; major exception reports (and the logic generating them); and how disclosure-related information is generated, including IT involvement.
Q.trap: Collapsing Risk assessment and Execution into one stage — ICAI's five-stage structure (with SA cross-references) is itself testable, independent of any fact pattern.

Q.q: A bank's investment portfolio includes securities bought with clear intent to hold to maturity, others routinely traded, and a residual pool available for sale. The audit team must confirm the classification and valuation framework, and specifically test for non-performing investments (NPIs). Explain what the auditor checks.
Q.a:
Classification: the entire investment portfolio must sit in one of three categories — HTM (Held to Maturity), HFT (Held for Trading), AFS (Available for Sale) — decided at the time of acquisition by the Board, ALCO or Investment Committee as evidenced by their decision; shifting from AFS to HTM requires Board approval.

Valuation: the auditor examines whether the bank's accounting/valuation method (including at year end) is appropriate, whether income from investments is properly accounted (especially where income is received electronically), whether any change in valuation method is adequately disclosed, and whether profit/loss on sale of investments is computed and accounted for correctly.

NPI test: an investment where interest/principal remains unpaid for more than 90 days is a Non-Performing Investment — income on it is not recognised, and the bank must make a provision for depreciation in its value.
Q.trap: Treating NPI purely as a classification label — the real audit consequence is the double effect (stop income recognition and provide for depreciation), both of which must be checked.

Q.q: A bank holds a corporate bond with a pre-determined interest rate, serviced regularly, and separately holds shares in a company that declared a dividend at its AGM in April (the bank's financial year having ended 31 March). The bank wants to recognise both the bond interest and the dividend as income for the year just ended, on an accrual basis. Advise.
Q.a:
Bond interest: income on bonds/debentures of corporate bodies can be accrued where the interest rate is pre-determined and interest is being serviced regularly (not in arrears) — so accruing this interest for the year just ended is permissible.

Dividend: dividend income may be accrued only once declared by the corporate body at its AGM, with the right to receive payment established. Here the AGM declaration happened in April, i.e. after the financial year ended 31 March — so accruing the dividend for the year just ended is not permissible; it belongs to the following year, or is recognised on realisation.

Conclusion: the bond interest can be accrued; the dividend cannot — the key distinguishing fact is the AGM declaration date relative to the balance-sheet date.
Q.trap: Treating all 'regularly paid' investment income alike — bond interest and dividend income follow genuinely different accrual tests (servicing regularity vs. AGM declaration timing).

Q.q: A bank's balance sheet shows: Tier I capital ₹850 crore; Tier II capital ₹300 crore; total risk-weighted assets (on-balance-sheet) ₹9,000 crore; risk-adjusted off-balance-sheet items ₹1,000 crore. Within its risk-weighted assets is a secured housing loan portfolio: ₹200 crore of loans up to ₹75 lakh each (50% risk weight) and ₹120 crore of loans above ₹75 lakh (75% risk weight), already included at full value in the ₹9,000 crore figure above the risk-weighting step. Compute the bank's CRAR and comment on compliance, and show how the housing-loan risk weighting works.
Q.a:
Housing-loan risk-weighting illustration: ₹200cr (≤₹75 lakh loans) × 50% = ₹100cr risk-weighted; ₹120cr (>₹75 lakh loans) × 75% = ₹90cr risk-weighted — i.e. these ₹320cr of loans contribute only ₹190cr to the risk-weighted-assets denominator, not their full book value, which is why risk weights matter to the CRAR computation.

CRAR: CRAR = Eligible Total Capital Funds ÷ (Risk-weighted assets + risk-adjusted off-balance-sheet items) × 100 = (₹850cr + ₹300cr) ÷ (₹9,000cr + ₹1,000cr) × 100 = ₹1,150cr ÷ ₹10,000cr × 100 = 11.5%.

Conclusion: 11.5% exceeds RBI's minimum CRAR of 9% — the bank is compliant, and comfortably so.
Q.trap: Computing CRAR off book value of assets instead of their risk-weighted value — the housing-loan example exists specifically to show why the two numbers differ.

Q.q: An NBFC-MFI's microfinance-loan book has fallen to 55% of its total assets (net of intangibles) for three consecutive quarters, and is trending down further. Explain the regulatory concept being tested and what the NBFC must do if the shortfall continues for one more quarter.
Q.a:
Concept: an NBFC-MFI must keep at least 60% of total assets (net of intangibles) deployed, on an ongoing basis, in 'microfinance loans' as defined under the RBI (Regulatory Framework for Microfinance Loans) Directions, 2022 (broadly, collateral-free loans to low-income households meeting notified eligibility conditions — the exact income ceiling is a regulatory figure to check against the current Master Direction rather than memorise). This asset test is what justifies the lighter prudential treatment an MFI gets versus an ordinary ICC.

Consequence of continued shortfall: if the 55% level persists for a fourth consecutive quarter, the NBFC-MFI must approach RBI with a remediation plan — it is not automatically reclassified or deregistered, but it must proactively engage with the regulator once the 4-quarter threshold is crossed.
Q.trap: Assuming a single quarter's shortfall triggers regulatory action — the rule specifically requires four consecutive quarters before the remediation-plan obligation arises.

Q.q: A bank has 40 branches. Branch A handles high-value treasury and forex operations with a history of control exceptions; Branch B is a small rural branch with simple savings/current-account business and a clean inspection record. The Chief Audit Executive must decide how Risk-Based Internal Audit (RBIA) coverage should differ between them. Explain the reasoning.
Q.a:
Reasoning: RBIA works by first identifying each branch's inherent business risk (the risk that comes from the nature and scale of its activities) and then assessing the effectiveness of controls mitigating that risk, to arrive at an overall business-risk / control-risk matrix per branch — the same logic SA 315 applies at engagement level, used here as a bank-wide planning tool.

Application: Branch A combines high inherent risk (treasury/forex, large values, complexity) with a history of control exceptions (weaker control effectiveness) — it sits in a high-risk cell of the matrix and should receive more frequent and more intensive RBIA coverage. Branch B combines low inherent risk (simple retail business) with clean inspection history (strong control effectiveness) — a low-risk cell, warranting less frequent, lighter-touch coverage, without abandoning audit altogether.
Q.trap: Allocating RBIA coverage by branch size or deposit value alone — the matrix explicitly combines inherent risk and control effectiveness, not a single size-based proxy.

Q.q: A bank's advance to a borrower has been an NPA for over a year. The bank is weighing a civil suit for recovery against invoking the SARFAESI Act, 2002. Explain what SARFAESI lets the bank do differently, and whether using it changes the advance's NPA classification/provisioning status.
Q.a:
What SARFAESI enables: a secured creditor (bank/eligible NBFC) can, after the borrower (already classified NPA) fails to repay within 60 days of a demand notice, take possession of and sell the secured asset directly — without first obtaining a civil-court decree. This is materially faster than a conventional civil suit, which requires a full trial and decree before execution.

Effect on classification/provisioning: SARFAESI is purely a recovery mechanism, operating once an account is already NPA — invoking it does not pause, reverse or otherwise change the account's existing asset classification or the provisioning already required under the ordinary IRAC norms. The two frameworks run in parallel: IRAC decides classification/provisioning throughout; SARFAESI is simply one available recovery route once NPA status already exists.
Q.trap: Assuming that initiating SARFAESI proceedings somehow 'resets' or suspends NPA provisioning — recovery action and asset classification are independent tracks.

Q.q: A bank's advances schedule splits credit into 'priority sector' and 'other' categories, and separately discloses a Priority Sector Lending (PSL) achievement certificate each year. As auditor, what exactly are you verifying when you examine this classification — and what are you not expected to do?
Q.a:
What the SM test covers: advances are disclosed and classified, among other angles, on a sectoral basis (priority sector vs. other/public sector) — RBI sets a target share of adjusted net bank credit that banks must direct toward priority sectors (agriculture, MSME, export credit, housing, education, social infrastructure, renewable energy and similar categories), with shortfalls typically routed into RIDF-type funds.

What the auditor verifies: that each advance has been correctly tagged to the sectoral category the loan's actual purpose/borrower profile supports, and that the PSL-achievement certificate/return is consistent with that underlying classification.

What the auditor is not expected to do: independently compute or validate the regulatory PSL target percentage itself — that figure is a live RBI number to be checked against the current Master Direction, not something to be reasoned out or memorised for an exam answer.
Q.trap: Trying to quote a specific PSL target percentage from memory — the auditor's job here is classification-accuracy verification, not reproducing a regulatory figure that changes over time.

Q.q: You are appointed statutory auditor of a co-operative bank. A colleague auditing a nationalised bank assumes the appointment process and reporting lines will be identical. Explain how a co-operative bank's audit differs.
Q.a:
Dual regulation: a co-operative bank sits under two regulatory regimes simultaneously — its incorporation, registration and day-to-day governance follow the Co-operative Societies Act, 1912 / the relevant State Co-operative Societies Act (via the Registrar of Co-operative Societies), while its banking-business prudential norms (licensing, CRR/SLR, NPA classification/provisioning, capital adequacy) follow the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (as applied to co-operative banks) and RBI directions.

Appointment: unlike a banking company (shareholders' AGM) or a nationalised bank (Board of Directors, with RBI approval), a co-operative bank's statutory auditor is typically appointed through the co-operative statute/Registrar's process, not the s.139–140 Companies Act machinery.

Reporting: alongside the usual bank-audit reporting (statutory report, LFAR etc. as applicable), an additional report may be required to the Registrar of Co-operative Societies — a reporting line a nationalised- or private-bank audit doesn't have.
Q.trap: Assuming co-operative-bank audit appointment and reporting mirror a company-form bank exactly — the co-operative statute layer is the distinguishing feature the colleague is missing.

Q.q: An analyst compares capital ratios of a bank. Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ₹4,500 crore; Additional Tier 1 (AT1) ₹1,000 crore; Tier 2 ₹1,500 crore; risk-weighted assets ₹60,000 crore; total exposure measure ₹1,25,000 crore. Compute the CET1 ratio, Tier 1 ratio, total capital ratio and the leverage ratio (Tier 1 ÷ exposure). Then management moves ₹10,000 crore of housing loans (50% risk weight) into commercial real estate (100%). Recompute the total capital ratio and comment on the RBI minimum of 9% used in the SM.
Q.a:
Concept: capital ratios divide different layers of capital by risk-weighted assets; the leverage ratio ignores risk weights.

MeasureWorkingResult
CET1 ratio4,500 ÷ 60,0007.50%
Tier 1 ratio(4,500 + 1,000) ÷ 60,0009.17%
Total capital ratio7,000 ÷ 60,00011.67%
Leverage ratio5,500 ÷ 1,25,0004.40%
RWA after shift60,000 + 10,000 × (100% − 50%) = 65,000
Total capital ratio after shift7,000 ÷ 65,00010.77%

Conclusion: the shift costs about 0.9 percentage points of capital ratio with no change in capital: same loans, riskier mix. Both before and after, the total ratio is above the SM's 9% bank minimum. Beyond the SM: CET1, AT1 and the leverage ratio are Basel III terms; the SM states only the 9% CRAR. Check RBI's current component minima before quoting them.
Q.trap: Using the same denominator for the leverage ratio. Leverage uses total exposure, not risk-weighted assets.
nums: Total capital ratio after the shift

Q.src: CFA-style (app-written) · expected credit loss vs prudential provision
Q.q: An Ind AS NBFC in the Middle Layer reports (₹ crore): Stage 1 loans 200 (12-month PD 1%, LGD 40%); Stage 2 loans 30 (lifetime PD 10%, LGD 40%); Stage 3 loan 20 (credit-impaired, PD 100%, LGD 25%), which has been NPA for 30 months with realisable security of 12. (a) Compute the total expected credit loss (ECL = exposure × PD × LGD). (b) Compute the provision under the prudential (IRAC) norms: standard assets at 0.40%, doubtful secured portion at the rate for the time as doubtful, unsecured portion at 100%. (c) What happens to the difference?
Q.a:
(a) ECL: Stage 1: 200 × 1% × 40% = 0.8. Stage 2: 30 × 10% × 40% = 1.2. Stage 3: 20 × 100% × 25% = 5.0. Total ECL = 7.0.

(b) Prudential provision: standard assets (Stage 1 and 2) 230 × 0.40% = 0.92. Stage 3 loan: Middle Layer, doubtful after 12 months, so 18 months as doubtful (between 1 and 3 years): unsecured 20 − 12 = 8 × 100% = 8.0; secured 12 × 30% = 3.6. Total = 0.92 + 8.0 + 3.6 = 12.52.

(c) ECL (7.0) is lower than the prudential provision (12.52). Under RBI's approach for Ind AS NBFCs the shortfall of 5.52 is transferred from profit to an Impairment Reserve. Beyond the SM: confirm the latest RBI wording on the Impairment Reserve; the numbers above use the SM's provisioning table.
Q.trap: Treating Stage 2 loans as NPAs under IRAC. Stage 2 is an accounting stage (significant increase in credit risk); under IRAC it is still a standard asset.

Q.q: A bank holds high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) of ₹8,100 crore. Over a 30-day stress: stable retail deposits ₹30,000 crore run off at 5%; less-stable retail deposits ₹20,000 crore at 10%; wholesale funding ₹25,000 crore at 40%. Expected inflows are ₹4,500 crore (assume inflows count in full, within the cap). (a) Compute the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (HQLA ÷ net cash outflows). (b) Is it at least 100%? (c) How does this differ from the SLR the SM describes?
Q.a:
ItemWorking₹ crore
Stable retail outflow30,000 × 5%1,500
Less-stable retail outflow20,000 × 10%2,000
Wholesale outflow25,000 × 40%10,000
Total outflows13,500
Net outflows13,500 − 4,5009,000

LCR = 8,100 ÷ 9,000 = 90%. Below 100%, a shortfall of ₹900 crore of HQLA.

Difference from SLR: SLR is a flat percentage of DTL held in approved liquid assets regardless of how fragile the funding is. LCR is stress-based: the same HQLA can be enough for a bank with sticky retail deposits and too little for one with flighty wholesale funding. Beyond the SM; run-off rates here are illustrative, check RBI's current LCR rules.
Q.trap: Dividing HQLA by total outflows instead of net outflows.

Q.q: An analyst has these figures (₹ crore): gross advances 50,000; gross NPAs 2,500; provisions held against NPAs 1,500; standard-asset provision 200 (shown separately as a contingent provision). Compute the gross NPA ratio, net NPA, net NPA ratio and provision coverage ratio. Should the standard-asset provision be netted?
Q.a:
MeasureWorkingResult
Gross NPA ratio2,500 ÷ 50,0005.00%
Net NPA2,500 − 1,5001,000
Net advances50,000 − 1,50048,500
Net NPA ratio1,000 ÷ 48,5002.06%
Provision coverage ratio1,500 ÷ 2,50060%

Standard-asset provision: no. It is shown separately and is never netted from gross advances nor reckoned in net-NPA arithmetic (the SM's NBFC provisioning rule). Netting it would understate net NPAs.
Q.trap: Using gross advances as the denominator of the net NPA ratio. Net NPA ratio uses net advances.

Q.src: CFA-style (app-written) · margin effect of an NPA
Q.q: A bank earned interest income of ₹6,000 crore and incurred interest expense of ₹3,600 crore on average earning assets of ₹40,000 crore. Included in income is ₹90 crore accrued on a ₹1,000 crore loan (12% for 9 months) that has just become an NPA with nothing realised. Compute the net interest margin (NIM) before and after the required treatment. Assume earning assets are unchanged.
Q.a:
Before: (6,000 − 3,600) ÷ 40,000 = 6.00%.

Treatment: on an NPA, interest is recognised only on realisation; the ₹90 crore credited but unrealised is reversed.

After: (6,000 − 90 − 3,600) ÷ 40,000 = 2,310 ÷ 40,000 = 5.775%. One bad loan costs about 0.23 percentage points of margin, and the NPA also stops earning from here on.
Q.trap: Leaving the accrued interest in income because it was "earned". On an NPA it is reversed.

Q.q: A bank and a non-deposit NBFC have the same loan book and similar profitability. The NBFC funds itself with market borrowings and commercial paper. An analyst asks why RBI regulates large NBFCs more heavily than small ones and why NBFCs are still treated differently from banks. Discuss with reference to funding risk, interconnectedness and regulatory arbitrage.
Q.a:
Funding risk: an NBFC has no insured retail deposits (no DICGC) and no access to demand deposits, so it depends on market funding that can disappear in stress. A run on its paper can force asset sales.

Interconnectedness: large NBFCs borrow from banks and mutual funds and lend to many borrowers; failure of one transmits to the rest. That is why the Upper Layer (top 10 by size plus RBI's scoring) faces tougher norms, and a Top Layer exists for the case where systemic risk rises sharply.

Regulatory arbitrage: when banks face CRR/SLR and 9% CRAR while NBFCs do not, lending can migrate to the lighter-regulated entity. Scale-based regulation (from 1 October 2022) narrows the gap as size and activity grow, while keeping Base Layer compliance light.

Still different from banks: no demand deposits, no payment-system role, no DICGC, no CRR/SLR, no priority-sector target. The NBFC capital bar (15%, Tier I 10%) is higher than the bank's 9% partly to compensate for the missing liquidity backstop.

The last sentence is an interpretation, not an SM statement.
Q.trap: Saying NBFCs are "unregulated". They are regulated by RBI under Chapter IIIB; what differs is the form.

Q.src: CFA-style (app-written) · reading audit findings like an analyst
Q.q: An analyst reading a bank's annual report notes these audit findings: (i) several accounts were regularised just before the balance-sheet date out of fresh bank funding; (ii) limits were repeatedly renewed for short ad hoc periods; (iii) the LFAR records title deeds held at a different office; (iv) concurrent audit flagged revenue leakage in interest calculations. Explain what each tells the analyst about asset quality, controls and earnings, and what the auditor should have tested.
Q.a:
(i) Evergreening risk (asset quality): regularising from fresh funding hides weakness. The auditor must test whether repayment came from genuine sources and whether the inherent weakness persists, before accepting a standard classification (bank-npa-class).

(ii) Dodging the 180-day rule (asset quality): repeated ad hoc or short reviews can be used to avoid classifying an account whose limit has not been reviewed within 180 days as an NPA. Test review dates, not only sanction letters.

(iii) Control weakness (security): title deeds elsewhere means the bank may not be able to enforce its security. This is the kind of branch-level item the LFAR records specifically.

(iv) Earnings quality: revenue leakage means interest, discount, commission or exchange was under-charged; concurrent audit percentage-checks these calculations. Analyst effect: reported margin understates earning power, but the control failure is a warning.
Q.trap: Treating regularisation near year end as proof of recovery without checking the source of funds.

Q.q: Two gold-loan NBFC-BLs each have RWA ₹1,000 crore. Lender A reports Tier I of ₹130 crore, which includes ₹25 crore of perpetual debt instruments. Lender B reports Tier I of ₹118 crore with no perpetual debt. Reported, A looks stronger. After the NBFC-BL rule on perpetual debt, compare their Tier I ratios with the 12% gold-loan floor.
Q.a:
Lender ALender B
Reported Tier I130118
Reported ratio13.0%11.8%
Perpetual debt (NBFC-BL cannot count)− 250
Adjusted Tier I105118
Adjusted ratio10.5%11.8%
12% floor = 120Short by 15Short by 2

Conclusion: the ranking reverses. B has higher quality capital; neither meets the 12% gold-loan floor. Always adjust reported Tier I for instruments the category cannot count.
Q.trap: Ranking lenders on reported Tier I. Quality of capital matters, not just the headline number.

Lender B adjusted Tier I ratio

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · FCNR interest
Q.q: One line in the SM says FCNR interest is calculated on a 360-day year and converted to rupees at the head-office notified rate, with the gain or loss taken to P&L. A bank holds an FCNR fixed deposit of US$ 50,000 at 2% p.a. Interest for 90 days is due. The HO notified rate is ₹84 per US$. Compute the interest in US$ and ₹, and state what an auditor checks.
Q.a:
Interest = 50,000 × 2% × 90 ÷ 360 = US$ 250. In rupees: 250 × 84 = ₹21,000.

Auditor checks: the day-count is 360, not 365; the rate used is the HO-notified rate; and the exchange difference is routed to the profit and loss account.
Q.trap: Using 365 days. That gives US$ 246.58 and a wrong ₹ figure.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · inoperative accounts
Q.q: The SM says an account with no transactions for over 2 years is inoperative, and that a significant balance drop compared with last year warrants checking authorisation. At year end an account inoperative for 3 years was revived on 20 March and ₹8 lakh was withdrawn from a balance of ₹8.5 lakh the same week. What will you check and what could it indicate?
Q.a:
Rule: inoperative status (no transaction for over 2 years); revival needs proper authority; a large fall in balance needs the withdrawal authorisation checked.

Checks: who authorised revival and on what documents (KYC, signature verification); whether the withdrawal was by the account holder or a mandated person; whether the cheque or form, signatures and identity were verified; how branch staff handled the dormant-account safeguards; confirmation from the customer.

Could indicate: fraud or misappropriation of dormant balances by insiders. If suspected, evaluate reporting duties (s.143(12), RBI).
Q.trap: Treating the withdrawal as routine because the balance was the customer's own.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · bulk deposit threshold
Q.q: The SM mentions bulk deposits of ₹2 crore and above for scheduled commercial banks. A branch accepted a ₹1.8 crore term deposit at the higher bulk rate, and a ₹3 crore deposit was closed before maturity with no penalty deducted. Comment.
Q.a:
₹1.8 crore: below the ₹2 crore bulk threshold, so the bulk (higher) rate was not available; interest paid in excess is a revenue leak and a control lapse.

₹3 crore: a bulk deposit, so the correct rate at acceptance should have been the bulk rate; premature closure requires the foreclosure penalty to be deducted. Not deducting it understates income.

Auditor action: recompute interest on both, quantify the excess/short, and report as an internal-control weakness; consider adjusting the financial statements if material.
Q.trap: Accepting the rate because it was approved at the branch. The threshold decides the rate.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · unbooked deposit interest in DTL
Q.q: The SM says interest accrued on deposits is part of DTL whether or not booked. Term deposits are ₹3,650 crore at 6% p.a.; interest has accrued for 45 days since it was last paid and is not yet booked. Compute the accrued interest (365-day year) and the extra CRR if CRR is 4%.
Q.a:
Accrued interest = 3,650 × 6% × 45 ÷ 365 = 3,650 ÷ 365 = 10; 10 × 6% × 45 = ₹27 crore.

This is added to DTL (even though unbooked), so extra CRR = 27 × 4% = ₹1.08 crore.
Q.trap: Ignoring the accrual because the books do not show it.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · cashier and ledger
Q.q: The SM says a cashier must have no access to the customer ledger or day book. Short of staff, a branch lets the cashier post the savings ledger "just for lunch hours". Cash shortages have been small but frequent. Advise the SCA on risk and on what to report.
Q.a:
Risk: a person who can both handle cash and alter the ledger can conceal misappropriation; small repeated shortages are a typical fingerprint of such concealment.

Rule: segregate custody of cash from record-keeping. Cash should be in joint custody of two officers and agreed to the day book daily by someone independent.

Actions: extend substantive tests on cash and customer accounts for the period; check ledger postings by the cashier; recommend withdrawing ledger access; include the lapse in the LFAR/internal-control report; if fraud is suspected, follow the fraud-reporting route.
Q.trap: Writing "staff shortage" as a mitigating factor. It explains the lapse; it does not cure the control weakness.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · ROU assets in NBFC risk weights
Q.q: The May 2026 update says right-of-use (ROU) assets sit in the "Others" line of the NBFC risk-weight table at 100%. A general NBFC has Tier I ₹100 crore, Tier II ₹50 crore and RWA ₹900 crore excluding ₹40 crore of ROU assets. Compute the capital ratio before and after adding the ROU assets, and comment on compliance with 15%.
Q.a:
Before: 150 ÷ 900 = 16.67%. ROU assets 40 × 100% = 40 added: RWA = 940. After: 150 ÷ 940 = 15.96%.

Still above 15% (and Tier I 100 ÷ 940 = 10.64%, above 10%), so compliant, but the cushion has shrunk by about 0.7 points. Excluding the ROU assets would overstate the ratio.
Q.trap: Treating ROU assets as zero-risk because they are leases, not loans.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · standard-asset provision and net NPA
Q.q: The SM says the standard-asset provision is shown separately and never reckoned in net-NPA arithmetic. An NBFC has gross advances ₹8,000 crore, NPAs ₹400 crore, provisions against NPAs ₹150 crore and a contingent provision against standard assets of ₹20 crore. Compute net NPA and the net NPA ratio.
Q.a:
Net NPA = 400 − 150 = ₹250 crore (the ₹20 crore standard-asset provision is ignored).

Net NPA ratio = 250 ÷ (8,000 − 150) = 250 ÷ 7,850 = 3.18%.
Q.trap: Deducting the standard-asset provision as well, giving 230 and a lower ratio.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · Central vs State guarantee
Q.q: The SM says a Central Government guaranteed advance is NPA only after the guarantee is invoked and repudiated, but not so for State guarantees. A bank has two advances, each overdue 120 days: A guaranteed by the Central Government (guarantee not yet invoked) and B guaranteed by a State Government. Classify each, and deal with interest income.
Q.a:
Account A (Central guarantee): not classified NPA merely because it is overdue; classification waits until the guarantee is invoked and repudiated.

Account B (State guarantee): follows the ordinary rule: overdue for more than 90 days means NPA.

Income on both: for income recognition, the guarantee does not help; interest is not taken to income unless realised.
Q.trap: Treating both guarantees alike. The carve-out is only for Central Government guarantees.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · bank receipts and SGL
Q.q: The SM says bank receipts (BRs) cannot be issued for government-securities deals where the SGL facility is available. At year end the bank holds BRs from a counterparty for ₹40 crore of G-secs bought two years ago, still not converted into SGL delivery. What does the auditor do?
Q.a:
Issue: BRs for G-sec deals where SGL is available are not permitted, and a BR outstanding two years is a long-outstanding BR.

Procedures: obtain counterparty confirmation of the BR; investigate why it is outstanding and whether the securities exist and are owned by the bank (existence and ownership); agree to SGL/depository statements; check valuation per RBI norms; report as a compliance and control lapse.

If unconfirmed: the ₹40 crore may not exist as an asset; consider qualification.
Q.trap: Accepting the BR as evidence of the securities themselves. A BR is a receipt, not the security.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · Tier II composition
Q.q: The SM says revaluation reserves count in Tier II after a 55% discount, and general provisions up to 1.25% of RWA. A general NBFC (not BL) has revaluation reserves ₹100 crore, general provisions ₹40 crore, subordinated debt ₹30 crore, RWA ₹2,000 crore and Tier I ₹120 crore. Compute eligible Tier II and check the cap.
Q.a:
ComponentWorking₹ crore
Revaluation reserves100 × (1 − 55%)45
General provisionscap 1.25% × 2,000 = 25; held 40, so 2525
Subordinated debt30
Total Tier II45 + 25 + 30100

Cap: Tier II (100) does not exceed Tier I (120), so the full amount counts.
Q.trap: Counting the full ₹40 crore of general provisions, or ignoring the revaluation discount.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · perpetual debt cap
Q.q: The SM caps perpetual debt in Tier I at 15% of the prior year's aggregate Tier I, with the excess going to Tier II. A general NBFC (not BL) had prior-year Tier I of ₹200 crore and has perpetual debt of ₹50 crore. How much counts in Tier I and how much is pushed to Tier II?
Q.a: Cap = 15% × 200 = ₹30 crore in Tier I. Excess = 50 − 30 = ₹20 crore, counted in Tier II (subject to the Tier II ≤ Tier I limit). For an NBFC-BL, the whole ₹50 crore would be excluded from both tiers.
Q.trap: Applying the 15% to current-year Tier I. The cap uses the prior year's aggregate Tier I.

Q.src: Built from one line of the SM (app-written) · Statutory Auditor's Certificate timing
Q.q: The SM says the Statutory Auditor's Certificate reaches RBI within 5 working days of signing the audit report, but not later than 31 December. An NBFC auditor signs the audit report on Friday 26 December 2025. By when must the certificate reach the DNBS regional office?
Q.a:
Five working days after 26 December would fall on or about 2 January 2026 (working days: 29, 30, 31 December, 1 and 2 January, ignoring local holidays). The outer limit is 31 December 2025, which is earlier, so the certificate must reach RBI by 31 December 2025.

Principle: both limits apply; the earlier binds.
Q.trap: Counting only the five working days. The 31 December ceiling can bite when the report is signed late in the year.

method: Identify the precise RBI direction, BR Act section, or Companies Act/CARO clause that decides the fact pattern — cite it the way the examiner expects (e.g. 'Clause (xvi) of Paragraph 3, CARO 2020', not just 'CARO').
Step 2 — Apply it to the facts

Give a clear verdict, figure, or advice, repeating the rule name. For a 'comment'/'advise' question, state explicitly whether the bank's/NBFC's/auditor's treatment is correct or not, and why.

Bank/NBFC chapter answers are checklist-heavy — ICAI's marking scheme typically awards one mark per correctly stated point, so write in short labelled sentences or a numbered/bulleted list rather than one flowing paragraph. formulas.title: Capital adequacy: resilience per unit of risk taken
formulas.idea: A bank or NBFC can't just hold whatever capital it likes — regulators tie the minimum capital to how risky its assets are. Riskier assets need more capital behind them. CRAR is simply: how much loss-absorbing capital do I have, for every rupee of risk I've taken on?

master.name: CRAR (Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio)
master.expr: CRAR = Eligible Total Capital Funds (Tier I + Tier II)Risk-weighted assets + risk-adjusted off-balance-sheet items × 100
master.logic: Think of risk-weighted assets as a 'danger score' for the balance sheet — a ₹100 cash balance scores 0 (perfectly safe), but a ₹100 unsecured personal loan scores much higher, because it's more likely to go bad. CRAR asks: for every rupee of that danger score, how many paise of real, loss-absorbing capital is standing behind it?
vars: highest-quality capital — share capital and disclosed reserves, fully available to absorb losses
lower-quality capital — certain reserves and subordinated debt, with weaker loss-absorption
master.hook: Capital ÷ danger-weighted assets, not capital ÷ book-value assets.
master.cue: "Compute CRAR", "capital adequacy ratio", "Tier I/Tier II capital", a risk-weighted-assets table.
master.trap: Dividing capital by the book value of assets instead of their risk-weighted value — a bank holding mostly cash and government securities needs far less capital than one holding the same book value in unsecured advances.
master.example: Secured housing loan ₹60 lakh at 50% risk weight → risk-weighted value ₹30 lakh (SM Example 4). A bank with Tier I ₹850cr, Tier II ₹300cr, RWA ₹9,000cr and off-balance-sheet risk-adjusted items ₹1,000cr: CRAR = (850+300)/(9,000+1,000)×100 = 1,150/10,000×100 = 11.5% — comfortably above the 9% bank minimum.

items.name: Converting book value into risk-weighted value
items.expr: Risk-weighted value of an asset = Book value × applicable risk weight %
vars: a percentage set by RBI per asset type — 0% for cash/government securities, up to 125% for retail/credit-card exposure
items.logic: Every asset on the balance sheet gets 'marked down' (or occasionally marked up) by how dangerous it is, before it counts toward the CRAR denominator.
items.derive: This is literally how the CRAR master formula's denominator is built, asset by asset, then summed.
items.hook: Safe assets barely count; risky assets count double (or more).
items.cue: A table of asset categories with risk-weight percentages; "aggregate risk-adjusted value of funded assets".
items.trap: Forgetting that some categories (e.g. State-Government-guaranteed claims) carry a different weight depending on a condition (in default vs not, and for how long) — read the condition before picking the %.
items.example: Easy Finance Ltd (PYQ Sep 2025): cash/bank ₹8cr×0%=0; PFI bonds ₹50cr×100%=₹50cr; staff loans ₹5cr×0%=0; furniture ₹30cr×100%=₹30cr; State-Govt-guaranteed claims in default ≤90 days ₹60cr×20%=₹12cr → total ₹92 crore.

items.name: NBFC Tier I floor — general vs gold-loan
items.expr: Required Tier I = Risk-weighted assets × 10% (general) or × 12% (gold-loan NBFC, ≥50% financial assets in gold loans)
vars: an NBFC whose loans against gold jewellery make up 50% or more of its financial assets
items.logic: Gold-loan books carry a concentration/collateral-liquidity risk RBI treats as warranting a thicker capital cushion — so the floor steps up from 10% to 12% once that 50% activity test is crossed.
items.derive: A specific instrument-quality floor sitting inside the master CRAR formula's 15%-total requirement for NBFCs (Tier I is the higher-quality half of that total).
items.hook: Gold loans ≥50% of financial assets → Tier I floor jumps from 10% to 12%.
items.cue: "NBFC primarily engaged in lending against gold jewellery", a stated % of financial assets in gold loans.
items.trap: Applying the 12% floor to every NBFC — it only applies once gold loans cross the 50%-of-financial-assets line; otherwise the general 10% floor governs.
items.example: Instant Finance Ltd (PYQ May 2025): gold loans 60% of financial assets (≥50%) → 12% × ₹1,000cr RWA = required Tier I ₹120 crore.

items.name: Tier I adjustments — perpetual debt and inter-NBFC investment
items.expr: Adjusted Tier I = Reported Tier I − (perpetual debt instruments, if NBFC-BL) − (investment in other NBFCs' shares/debt exceeding 10% of owned fund)
vars: paid-up capital plus free reserves, reduced by accumulated losses/intangibles
items.logic: Capital that's really just debt dressed up (perpetual debt, for a Base-Layer NBFC) or capital that's really tied up propping up another NBFC (investment beyond 10% of owned fund in other NBFCs) doesn't genuinely strengthen *this* company's ability to absorb its own losses — so both get stripped back out.
items.derive: Reduces the numerator the nbfc-tier1-floor item tests against.
items.hook: NBFC-BL: no perpetual debt in Tier I at all. Any NBFC: inter-NBFC investment over 10% of owned fund comes straight back out.
items.cue: "Reported Tier I capital includes perpetual debt instruments"; "investment in shares/bonds of other NBFCs … % of owned fund".
items.trap: Applying the perpetual-debt exclusion to a non-BL NBFC — only NBFC-BL is barred from counting perpetual debt in Tier I at all; other NBFCs may include it up to 15% of the prior year's aggregate Tier I.
items.example: Instant Finance Ltd (NBFC-BL): reported Tier I ₹130cr includes ₹15cr perpetual debt → excluded entirely → ₹115cr. Owned fund = ₹10cr ÷ 12% = ₹83.33cr; 10% threshold = ₹8.33cr; excess investment = ₹10cr − ₹8.33cr = ₹1.667cr further deducted → ₹113.33cr. Either way, below the ₹120cr requirement → non-compliant.

formulas.title: DTL: the real base for CRR and SLR
formulas.idea: CRR and SLR are percentages of something — and that something (Demand and Time Liabilities) isn't just whatever number the bank's books happen to show. RBI has its own list of what must be added back in and taken back out before you apply the percentage.

master.name: Corrected DTL
master.expr: DTL = Reported liability figure − Σ(excluded items) + Σ(included-but-unbooked items)
master.logic: Imagine totting up your household's 'amount owed to others' for a loan application — you wouldn't count your own savings as a debt (even if it sits in the same bank statement), but you *would* add in a bill you know is coming even if you haven't paid it yet. DTL works the same way: strip out things that aren't really liabilities to outsiders, add in things that are liabilities even though not yet booked.
vars: paid-up capital, reserves, P&L credit balance, RBI/EXIM/NHB/NABARD/SIDBI borrowings, bad-debt recoveries, sundry-deposit margins, and similar — see the bank-dtl provision for the full list
net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts; interest accrued on deposits each reporting fortnight, whether or not yet booked
master.hook: Start from the reported number, then subtract the "not really ours to owe" items and add the "we owe it, just haven't booked it yet" items.
master.cue: "DTL balance … which included the following", a list of items to examine for CRR/SLR compliance.
master.trap: Treating every listed item the same way — some genuinely need subtracting out, others (branch-adjustment credit balance, unbooked interest accrued) are correctly already part of DTL and need no adjustment.
master.example: Maha Bank Ltd (PYQ Nov 2024): reported DTL ₹50,000cr; exclude paid-up capital ₹27,000cr + reserves ₹1,650cr + P&L credit ₹1,210cr + RBI loan ₹575cr + EXIM/NHB refinance ₹480cr + bad-debt recoveries ₹125cr + sundry-deposit margins ₹80cr = ₹31,120cr; branch-adjustment credit balance (₹105cr) and unbooked interest accrued (₹90cr) need no further adjustment (already counted) → corrected DTL = 50,000 − 31,120 = ₹18,880 crore.

items.name: Minimum cash reserve / liquid assets from DTL
items.expr: Minimum CRR cash = CRR% × DTL; Minimum SLR liquid assets = SLR% × DTL
vars: rates RBI sets from time to time — check the current Master Circular rather than quoting a memorised figure
items.logic: Once DTL is correctly computed, applying the RBI-notified percentage is simple arithmetic — the hard part was always getting DTL right, not the multiplication.
items.derive: Direct application of the DTL master figure.
items.hook: Get DTL right first — the CRR/SLR percentage itself is the easy part.
items.cue: "Compute the minimum CRR/SLR requirement", given a DTL figure and a notified rate.
items.trap: Applying the CRR/SLR percentage to the uncorrected reported liability figure instead of the corrected DTL.
items.example: If corrected DTL is ₹18,880cr and the notified CRR rate is (say) 4%, minimum CRR cash = 4% × 18,880 = ₹755.2 crore — illustrative only; always use the rate in force for the attempt.

formulas.title: Drawing power: what the bank will actually lend against today
formulas.idea: A sanctioned limit is the ceiling; drawing power is the floor of what's actually, currently, safely available — based on what security genuinely exists right now, not what was sanctioned once.

master.name: Drawing Power (DP)
master.expr: DP = [Eligible stock × (1 − stock margin %)] + [Eligible debtors × (1 − debtor margin %)], capped at the sanctioned limit
master.logic: Picture security as a pile of coins the bank can fall back on if the borrower can't pay. You don't count coins that are damaged (bad stock), already promised to someone else (creditors for that stock), or too old to trust (debtors overdue beyond the agreed period) — and even on the good coins, you keep a safety margin, lending only part of their value.
vars: paid-for stock in saleable condition, net of any sundry creditors for that stock already availed
debtors within the sanctioned ageing limit (e.g. excluding those overdue beyond 90 days), net of bills discounted with banks
master.hook: Good stock and good debtors only, each shaved by its margin — then check the sanctioned-limit cap.
master.cue: "Compute the Drawing Power", a stock/debtors schedule with margins and a sanctioned limit.
master.trap: Forgetting to net stock value against sundry creditors for that very stock — declared stock cannot cover a liability the borrower already owes suppliers for the same goods.
master.example: Kiran Ltd (PYQ May 2025): stock ₹900L (₹60L damaged) less creditors ₹140L = ₹700L eligible, ×75% (25% margin) = ₹525L. Debtors ₹800L less ₹100L overdue beyond 90 days = ₹700L eligible, ×60% (40% margin) = ₹420L. DP = 525+420 = ₹945 lakh.

formulas.title: Provisioning: how much of a bad loan to book today
formulas.idea: The worse an asset's credit quality, and the longer it's stayed bad, the more of it must be provided for — provisioning scales with both category and, within Doubtful, with how long it's been doubtful.

master.name: NBFC provisioning by asset category
master.expr: Loss: 100% of outstanding · Doubtful: 100% of unsecured portion + (20% / 30% / 50% of secured portion, by age doubtful ≤1yr / 1–3yrs / >3yrs) · Sub-standard: 10% flat · Standard: 0.25% (NBFC-BL) / 0.40% (not NBFC-UL)
master.logic: Think of it like a shrinking promise: a Standard loan is almost certainly fine (tiny provision), a Sub-standard one has started wobbling (a flat cushion), a Doubtful one has an unsecured piece that's basically already lost (100% there) plus a secured piece whose recoverable value erodes the longer it drags on (so the % climbs with age), and a Loss asset is one everyone already agrees is gone (100%, full stop).
vars: the part of the outstanding covered by the realisable value of security the NBFC has valid recourse to
outstanding minus the realisable security value
master.hook: Loss = all gone. Doubtful = unsecured gone + secured fading with age (20→30→50%). Sub-standard = flat 10%. Standard = a sliver, just in case.
master.cue: "Compute the provision required", an asset classified Doubtful/Loss with a stated security value and NPA date.
master.trap: Provisioning the secured portion at 100% once an asset is Doubtful — only the unsecured portion gets 100%; the secured portion only gets the tiered 20/30/50% by age.
master.example: RR Traders (PYQ Jan 2026): outstanding ₹3.8cr, realisable security ₹2.2cr → unsecured ₹1.6cr × 100% = ₹1.6cr; secured ₹2.2cr, doubtful for under a year × 20% = ₹0.44cr; total provision = ₹2.04 crore.

items.name: How long an account has actually been Doubtful
items.expr: Years doubtful = (Balance-sheet date − date the account crossed from Sub-standard into Doubtful) in whole years
vars: NPA date + the sub-standard-to-doubtful cut (12 months for NBFC-ML/above, 18 months for NBFC-BL)
items.logic: The age-tier clock for the secured portion starts only once the account actually becomes Doubtful — not from its original NPA date.
items.derive: Feeds the age-bucket (20/30/50%) in the master formula's Doubtful line.
items.hook: NPA date + 12 (or 18) months = the date the Doubtful clock itself starts ticking.
items.cue: An NPA date is given, and you're asked for the current year's provisioning percentage on the secured portion.
items.trap: Measuring 'years doubtful' from the original NPA date instead of from the later date the account actually crossed into the Doubtful category.
items.example: RR Traders: NPA from 1.9.2023; NBFC-ML 12-month cut → Doubtful from ~1.9.2024; by 31.3.2025 that's under 1 year doubtful → 20% tier applies to the secured portion.

items.name: Consortium account — interest to reverse
items.expr: Interest to reverse = Interest debited to the borrower's account − Credits actually received, over the period under review
vars: several banks lending jointly to one large borrower under a lead bank, each classifying its own share independently
items.logic: If what's coming in from the borrower is less than what's being charged as interest, the shortfall is unrealised income sitting on the books that must come back out — regardless of what the lead bank's certificate says about the account's status.
items.derive: A bank-side mirror of the master formula's realisation principle — reverse what hasn't actually been received.
items.hook: Each consortium member classifies and reverses on its OWN recovery experience, never on the lead bank's say-so.
items.cue: A consortium cash-credit account, a lead bank's 'performing' certificate, and a stated interest-debit vs. credit-received gap.
items.trap: Deferring to the lead bank's classification certificate — each member bank must classify (and reverse income) independently.
items.example: X Ltd consortium account (SM TYK 5): interest debited ₹1.75cr, credits received ₹1.25cr over two quarters → ₹0.50cr must be reversed and the account shown as NPA, despite the lead bank's 'performing' certificate.

items.name: NPA sale — which accounts actually qualify
items.expr: Eligible for sale = every proposed NPA where (Sale year − NPA financial year) ≥ 2 years
vars: the financial year in which the account first became NPA, not any later calendar date
items.logic: A bank can't offload an NPA the moment it turns bad — it has to have genuinely tried and failed with that asset for a minimum stretch of time (2 years) before passing it on.
items.derive: A gatekeeping test that has to be cleared before the master formula's sale-accounting rules (no profit booked, no provision reversed above NBV) even apply.
items.hook: 2 years in the NPA books, counted from the NPA's own financial year, not from today's calendar date.
items.cue: A table of proposed NPAs for sale, each with its own 'NPA since FY …' tag, and a sale date.
items.trap: Counting from the oldest-looking entry instead of checking each account's own NPA-since year against the 2-year cut.
items.example: NRF Bank Ltd (SM TYK 14), proposing sale in April 2024: Fin Pvt. Ltd. (2020-21), Book Store (2019-20), Fancy Corp. (2018-19) and RSM and Associates (2021-22) all clear 2 years; Dairy Works (2022-23) does not — total eligible ₹36.55+29.85+61.42+19.25 = ₹147.07 lakh.

formulas.title: Is it even an NBFC? The principal-business test
formulas.idea: Before any prudential rule applies, a company has to clear a gate: is lending/investing actually its main business, judged from its own last audited balance sheet, on both the asset side and the income side?

master.name: Principal-business test (both limbs required)
master.expr: NBFC if: Financial assetsTotal assets (net of intangibles) > 50% AND Income from financial assetsGross income > 50%
master.logic: Imagine a shop that also runs a small money-lending side business. It's only really a 'money-lending company' if lending makes up most of what it owns and most of what it earns — if it owns mostly loan assets but earns most of its money from trading, it's still fundamentally a trading company.
vars: loans/advances, investments in securities, and similar — netted against intangible assets on the total-assets side
total income including trading/other operational income, not only financial-asset income
master.hook: Both legs must clear 50% — one leg failing sinks the whole test.
master.cue: "Is the company an NBFC?", "advise on registration under s.45-IA", a balance-sheet/income extract to test.
master.trap: Concluding NBFC status from the asset-side test alone — Satyam Pvt Ltd (SM TYK) clears the asset test but fails the income test, and is therefore not an NBFC.
master.example: Singh Ltd (SM TYK Q12): financial assets ₹374cr ÷ total assets net of intangibles ₹608cr = 61.5%; income from financial assets ₹68cr ÷ gross income ₹118.75cr = 57.3%. Both >50% → qualifies as an NBFC.

items.name: NOF adequacy — a second gate, after the principal-business test
items.expr: NOF-compliant if Net Owned Fund held ≥ RBI-notified minimum NOF for that NBFC category
vars: paid-up capital plus free reserves, less accumulated losses/intangibles and certain other deductions
items.logic: Clearing the principal-business test only tells you the company IS an NBFC in substance — it still needs enough of its own skin in the game (NOF) before RBI will actually grant registration.
items.derive: A second, independent gate applied after the master formula's principal-business test is passed.
items.hook: Principal-business test says WHAT it is; the NOF test says whether it's allowed to register as one yet.
items.cue: A stated Net Owned Fund figure, alongside a question about registration or CARO 2020 clause 3(xvi)(a).
items.trap: Treating a pending registration application as equivalent to being registered — CARO 2020 asks whether registration has actually been obtained.
items.example: Abhimanyu Finance Ltd (SM TYK Q10): NOF held ₹1.50cr against the then-prescribed ₹2cr minimum, and no CoR obtained (only applied for) — reportable under CARO 2020 Clause 3(xvi)(a).

items.name: Division III's 1%-of-total-income disclosure test
items.expr: Separate note required if: Item of other income/expenditure > 1% × Total income
vars: revenue from operations plus other income — not merely revenue from operations
items.logic: Same shape as the principal-business test (a figure measured against a 50%/1% line before the regulatory consequence kicks in) — except here the question is disclosure granularity, not NBFC status itself, and the base is total income, not revenue from operations.
items.derive: A sibling threshold test to the master formula's 50% lines, but for Schedule III disclosure rather than NBFC classification.
items.hook: Division III's 1% line is measured against total income — Division II's equivalent line uses revenue from operations (or ₹10 lakh, whichever is higher) instead.
items.cue: An 'other expenditure'/'other income' figure, alongside a total-income figure, under Division III of Schedule III.
items.trap: Testing the figure against 1% of revenue from operations (the Division II rule) instead of 1% of total income (the Division III rule).
items.example: An Ind-AS NBFC-D (SM TYU u2-3): manpower outsourcing cost ₹99.50cr against total income ₹10,000cr → 1% line = ₹100cr; ₹99.50cr is just under it, so no separate note is required.

formulas.title: Interest on a day count: accrued, FCNR and reversal
formulas.idea: Every interest figure in this chapter is principal × rate × days ÷ year. Only the day-count (360 or 365) and the question being asked change.

master.name: Interest for a part-year
vars: days since interest was last paid or booked
master.logic: A year of interest is P × r. If only 45 days have passed you earned 45/365 of that year. The "year basis" is just how many days the bank counts in a year.
master.cue: accrued interest for N days; interest on a deposit for part of a year
master.trap: Using 365 for FCNR, or forgetting that unbooked accrued interest still counts in DTL.

items.name: FCNR interest (360-day year)
items.logic: Same idea, but the SM says FCNR counts a 360-day year; convert at the HO-notified rate.
items.cue: FCNR deposit; foreign currency deposit interest

items.name: Interest reversed on turning NPA
items.expr: Reversal = interest credited but not realised
vars: accrued income taken to P&L earlier
items.logic: Once an account is NPA, income counts only when cash comes in. Anything booked but unpaid is taken back out.
items.derive: Master gives the accrual (P × r × days ÷ 365); NPA status reverses it.
items.cue: account becomes NPA; interest already credited; interest not realised
items.trap: Leaving the accrual in income because it was earned.
items.example: ₹1,000 crore × 12% × 9/12 = ₹90 crore reversed; NIM falls from 6.00% to 5.775% (CF5).
